fallback.title: Give us a few more hints
fallback.body: Even the editor needs a clue sometimes. Below is the whole 101-game shelf, alphabetical.

mood.label: Mood
mood.q1: How is your energy right now?

skill.label: Skill
skill.q1: How comfortable are you with card games?
skill.q2: Do you enjoy learning new rules?

social.label: Players
social.q1: Who do you want to play with?
social.q2: How heavy do you want the game to feel?

theme.label: Vibe
theme.q1: Which world do you want to be in?

skill.learning_rules: I want to learn new rules

blurb.accordion: Compact into one column. Completing it is rare — the journey is the point.
blurb.acesup: Four piles, one rule: ditch the lower same-suit card. Pure luck, lightning-fast rounds.
blurb.agnes: Klondike-style staircase columns meet a Canfield base rank. Pack down by same color, build up from the base — a tight, no-redeal challenge.
blurb.alaska: A Yukon variant that builds up or down by suit, with empty columns open to any card.
blurb.allfours: All Fours (Seven Up). A classic English 2-player trick-taker: deal 6 cards each and flip a turn-up for trump. The non-dealer stands or begs; on a beg the dealer gifts a point or runs the cards for a fresh trump. Win must-follow tricks to claim High, Low, Jack and Game; first to 7 points wins. A tight, decision-rich duel.
blurb.aluette: A Breton (Vendée) 4-player trick-taker in fixed 2v2 teams on a 48-card Spanish-suited pack. **It has no trump suit and no follow obligation, and strength is per CARD rather than per rank** -- six named cards, the *luettes*, outrank the whole deck: Monsieur (3 of coins) > Madame (3 of cups) > Borgne (2 of cups) > Vache (2 of coins) > Grand Neuf (9 of cups) > Petit Neuf (9 of coins). The same value can therefore be the best card in the deck in one suit and ordinary in another, so the ranking table is shown on screen at all times. Every other card ranks 3 > 2 > A > rey > caballo > sota > 9 > 8 > 7 > 6 > 5 > 4 with suit ignored, and equal ranks do not steal -- the card played first wins. Five tricks make a mène and taking three of them scores a point; the first team to the target score wins.
blurb.americantoad: Two-deck Canfield with a 20-card reserve: foundations circle round from whatever rank the deal turns up.
blurb.anaconda: Anaconda (Pass the Trash). A wild home-poker pot game: you are dealt 7 cards, then pass 3, then 2, then 1 to the left before keeping your best 5. The kept hand is revealed one card at a time, with a betting round of call/raise/fold between each reveal. The best 5-card poker hand still in the pot wins. Reading what your neighbours passed you is half the game.
blurb.andarbahar: Bet on which of two columns draws the joker's rank first. From India; the rules fit in one line.
blurb.auldlangsyne: The four Aces start as foundations; the rest deals four at a time onto four wastes to build A-K.
blurb.baccarat: Bet Player or Banker — that's it. The shortest rules in the casino. For nights when you want to ride the flow.
blurb.badugi: Four off-suit lows. Short and deep. The kind people become obsessed with.
blurb.bakersdozen: No-shuffle, deterministic. The pleasure of reading a solvable board.
blurb.bakersgame: FreeCell's ancestor. Same-suit stacking only — a tougher test for confident solvers.
blurb.baloot: The Gulf's most-played 32-card partnership game. Sun (no trump) and Hokom (trump) swap the rank order itself.
blurb.banluck: A Lunar New Year staple. Card count decides the rank, and only the banker is forced to draw.
blurb.barbu: A French compendium of 7 mini trick games. Each dealer picks a different contract — avoid hearts, dodge queens, or race to shed in 7s.
blurb.baseballpoker: 3s and 9s are wild. A face-up 4 pays you a card; a face-up 3 charges you the whole pot.
blurb.basra: An Egyptian/Levantine fishing (capture) game on a 52-card deck. Four players (you + 3 CPU, individual scoring) are each dealt four cards with four face-up on the table. A played number card captures table cards of the same rank and any subset whose values sum to it (multiple groups at once); Queens and Kings capture only by matching rank; a Jack sweeps the whole table except other Jacks. Clearing the table with a single non-Jack card scores a 'Basra' bonus (+10). Fresh hands are dealt until the stock runs out, and leftover table cards go to the last player who captured. Score the most cards, the 7♦, the 10♦, each Ace, and every Basra — highest total wins.
blurb.bauernschnapsen: An Austrian team game in the Schnapsen family. All 20 cards are dealt, each seat bids a contract (Rufer / Farbenzwang / Bettel), and following suit is mandatory from the first trick.
blurb.beggarmyneighbour: Beggar-My-Neighbour. Split 52 cards evenly; take turns playing one card face-up to a central pile. Penalty cards (J=1, Q=2, K=3, A=4) force the opponent to pay that many cards — but if a new penalty appears mid-payment the obligation flips back. Collect all 52 to win. Pure luck but penalty chains can stretch surprisingly long.
blurb.beleagueredcastle: Eight columns of castle to dismantle. A clear board for math-minded players.
blurb.coinche: Belote with an auction and a doubling ladder bolted on. All 32 cards are dealt, then the table **bids a target and a trump suit** (80 to 180 in tens, topped by Capot for all eight tricks). **The round is judged against the bid, not the opponents** - out-scoring the other side counts for nothing if the declared target was missed by one. The defenders may "coinche" to double the stake, and the declarers answer with "surcoinche" to double it again.
blurb.belote: France's national card game. Bells and announces give it unmistakable character.
blurb.bezique: A 2-player French trick game and the ancestor of Pinochle, played with a 64-card deck. In phase 1 (while the stock remains), the winner of each trick may declare one meld for points — marriage (20), royal marriage (40), Bezique ♠Q+♦J (40), four aces (100), kings (80), queens (60), or jacks (40) — then both players draw. When the stock empties, phase 2 is strict must-follow with no melds and a +10 last-trick bonus. Scores accumulate across deals to a target (default 1000); the higher total wins.
blurb.bhabhi: India and Pakistan, 3-7 players. Miss the suit and take the pile; last one holding cards loses.
blurb.bideuchre: An auction euchre where the whole 24-card pack is dealt out, so there is no kitty. The dealer alone may take the contract by equalling the bid.
blurb.bidwhist: A beloved American 4-player partnership trick-taker. Bid for trump and the direction of card strength (Uptown/Downtown); two jokers are the top trumps, with a 6-card kitty exchange.
blurb.bigben: A two-deck solitaire whose twelve foundations form a clock face, each finished when it shows its own hour.
blurb.bigo: Five hole cards Omaha — "Big O". Combinations explode and nut hands clash hard.
blurb.bigohilo: Big O with hi/lo split. Five cards, two directions — peak volatility.
blurb.bigtwo: Hong Kong's signature shedding game. Poker-hand combos meet climbing mechanics.
blurb.bisley: An open solitaire with all 52 cards face-up: the Aces start on the board and the King foundations open as you play them.
blurb.blackhole: A logic-puzzle patience by David Parlett. The Ace of Spades seeds a central black hole; the other 51 cards are dealt into 17 fans of three. Play any fan top whose rank is one away from the black hole top (any suit, no King-Ace wrap). Absorb all 52 cards to win. With no stock and everything visible, it plays as a pure look-ahead puzzle.
blurb.blackjack: A duel with the dealer for 21. The tension delivers in five minutes; the classic that never ages. Start here if unsure.
blurb.blackjackswitch: Play two hands; swap your second cards. The 'I should've taken the other one first' fun.
blurb.boston: The 18th-century Whist derivative. Fifteen bids from five tricks up to a slam, with the misere contracts slotted in between them.
blurb.botifarra: A Catalan partnership game with no auction — and you must win the trick if you can.
blurb.bouillotte: Bouillotte. An 18th-century French 3-card poker-vying pot game. Each player antes, is dealt 3 cards, and a shared 'retourne' card is turned up. Players take turns to call, raise (vie), or fold; when betting closes the non-folded players reveal their hands and the best hand — a brelan of three matching ranks (counting the retourne) beats a high card — takes the pot. A salon classic of bluff and nerve.
blurb.bourre: A Louisiana gambling classic fusing poker betting with trick-taking. Ante, choose to play or fold, swap cards, then battle must-follow tricks — win none and you're 'bourréd', owing the whole pot.
blurb.braid: A two-deck solitaire built around a twenty-card braid. You choose once, at the start, whether the foundations build up or down.
blurb.bridge: The pinnacle of trick-taking. A bidding language plus long-form strategy. Settle in.
blurb.briscola: Italy's tavern game. Points and trumps in pleasing balance, with a light tempo.
blurb.bristol: A tactical solitaire: build down any suit across eight columns, juggle three fan piles, and race the foundations up from Ace to King.
blurb.brusquembille: Play anything while the stock lasts; once it runs dry you must follow suit. What you threw away early decides the endgame in this 17th-century French ancestor.
blurb.bura: A Russian 36-card trick game: lead up to three cards of one suit at a time, and win by claiming 31 card points yourself.
blurb.burraco: Canasta's Italian cousin: empty your hand to claim an 11-card pozzetto.
blurb.calabresella: A Calabrian/Italian three-player trick-taker from the Tressette family, played with a 40-card deck. One Soloist bids chiamo or solo for the right to take the four-card monte and discard down to twelve, then plays alone against the coalition of the other two. There is no trump — you must follow the led suit — and rank runs 3>2>A>K>Q>J>7>6>5>4. Points are scored in thirds (A=3, 2/3/J/Q/K=1) plus a last-trick bonus, 33 thirds per deal, and the Soloist must take more than half to win. Stakes transfer and the first to 21 wins the match.
blurb.callbreak: South Asia's go-to four-player. Call (bid) and break (take) interplay shines.
blurb.canasta: A long-form South-American Rummy. Massive melds; sit-down sessions.
blurb.canfield: Born in an 1873 casino. High difficulty, high satisfaction.
blurb.caribbeandraw: A Caribbean Stud table with a **draw**: exchange up to two of your five cards for a fee equal to the ante before you decide to call. A free exchange would make drawing always correct, so the fee is what gives that decision weight. The dealer also qualifies on a tougher rule — a pair of 8s or better, so an A-K high dealer will not play you.
blurb.caribbeanstud: Stud poker against the dealer, with a progressive jackpot — the casino's classic shot at glory.
blurb.carioca: Carioca. A South American (Chilean/Brazilian) contract-rummy game played over seven rounds with a double deck plus wild jokers. Each round sets a stricter contract of melds — sets (tríos of matching ranks) and runs (escalas of same-suit sequences) — that you must lay down before you can go out. Draw from the stock or discard, build the required melds, then discard to end your turn; the first player to shed every card ends the round and everyone else scores the pips left in hand. After seven rounds the lowest total wins — a sociable, escalating rummy classic.
blurb.casinoholdem: Hold'em against the dealer. Community-card reads still apply — without any human-opponent stress.
blurb.casinowar: Hi-card wins, dealer-style War. Three seconds of rules, zero strategy, pure luck.
blurb.cassino: A Mediterranean fishing game. 'Capture' floor cards; the scoring feels craft-like.
blurb.catchten: A Scottish 36-card partnership game where you race to capture the trump honors — the Jack and Ten are gold.
blurb.cego: A 4-player trick-taker from Germany's Baden region on the 54-card tarock deck (four 8-card suits with J/C/Q/K courts, 21 numbered trumps, and the Sküs). You are seat 0. The declarer who wins the auction chooses a contract — Cego (keep just one card, lay down the other ten, and take the 10-card blind as a gamble) or Handspiel (keep the dealt hand) — and plays 1-vs-3 against the other three. Play follows suit, then trump, with the highest trump winning. The declarer makes the contract by capturing more than half of the card-points (54+). Deals settle zero-sum, and the highest cumulative score after the set deals wins.
blurb.chemindefer: The ancestor of baccarat: the bank travels the table and the third card is your call.
blurb.chinchon: A Spanish Gin Rummy cousin. 40-card deck, seven-card hands; cut your deadwood and knock. A same-suit run of all seven cards, the chinchon, wins instantly. For 2 to 4 players: pass the elimination limit and you are out, last one standing wins.
blurb.chinesepoker: Thirteen cards split into three hands — a puzzle-heavy casino poker. Chase scoops and royalties.
blurb.chineseten: A Chinese fishing game: A-9 capture by summing to ten, 10-K by rank, one card at a time, and only the red cards score.
blurb.cinch: A four-player (you + 3 CPU, individual scoring) All-Fours/Pitch-family bidding trick-taker on a 52-card deck. Nine cards are dealt to each player; players bid 0 (pass) to 14, and the high bidder names trump and leads. You must follow the led suit, but trump may be played at any time. Fourteen points per deal are exchanged — A/K/10/J of trump = 1 each, the Right Pedro (5 of trump) = 5, and the Left Pedro (off-5 of the same color) = 5 — and the bidding side is set back if it fails to make its bid. The first player to reach 21 wins.
blurb.cincinnati: Best five of ten — five in hand, five on the board, and the board is optional.
blurb.clocksolitaire: Lay cards on a clock face. Pure luck; pure brief diversion.
blurb.colorado: 104 cards, 20 piles, and eight foundations — half of them building down from the King. The waste goes on any pile, burying what was under it.
blurb.colourwhist: A Flemish contract whist where three aces settle the contract without an auction.
blurb.congress: Eight piles flank eight foundations in this two-deck game: build down ignoring suit, one card at a time.
blurb.conquian: The Mexican ancestor of Rummy. A 40-card duel where you race to lay down all your cards as table melds, and a card you take from the discard must be used at once.
blurb.contractrummy: A different contract (meld) each round. More rules — more depth.
blurb.courchevel: Five-card Omaha with the first flop card already face up before the opening bet.
blurb.courtpiece: A South-Asian 2-team trick-taker (also called Rang). Four players (seats 0&2 vs 1&3) get 13 cards each from a 52-card deck and play 13 tricks. The caller (Hakim) peeks at the first 5 cards and declares a trump suit — no numeric bidding. Play is must-follow, ace high, and trumps beat plain cards. A team taking 7 or more of the 13 tricks wins the round and scores a Sar (+1 point); sweeping all 13 tricks or winning consecutive rounds adds a Court bonus (+2). The first team to the point limit (default 7) wins.
blurb.crazyeights: UNO's ancestor. Eights are wild; suit-swaps generations have argued over.
blurb.crazyfourpoker: Poker where your best four of five play, and a strong hand lets you triple the bet.
blurb.crazypineapple: Pineapple with a post-flop discard. One more strategic curveball.
blurb.crazyquilt: Prise cards out of an 8x8 quilt, but only where a short side is exposed — an open long side frees nothing.
blurb.crescent: Sixteen columns shaped like a crescent. A handsome mid-form classic.
blurb.cribbage: An English Rummy played on a peg board. Fifteens and 31s for the brain.
blurb.cribbagesquares: Place 16 cards in a 4x4 grid, then turn a 17th; all four rows and four columns are scored as cribbage hands against it. 61 points clears it.
blurb.cruel: Cruel by name, cruel by play. Highly random short-form solitaire.
blurb.cuarenta: Ecuador's national card game for 4 players in 2 teams (seats {0,2}=Team A / {1,3}=Team B), played with a 40-card deck (no 8, 9 or 10). Each player is dealt 5 cards and 4 are placed on the table to start. On your turn you play one card: if it matches the rank of any table card you capture all matching cards, otherwise it is laid on the table. Immediately capturing the card the previous player just laid scores a caída (+2); capturing a run of three or more of a rank (ronda) scores extra points; clearing the whole table scores a limpia (+1). At round end the team that captured the majority (21+ of the 40 cards) earns a +6 most-cards bonus. The first team to reach the target score (40 by default) wins.
blurb.cuckoo: A 4-player life-survival game from Europe (also known as Chase the Ace or Ranter-Go-Round). Each player holds a single card and three lives. On your turn you keep your card or swap it with your neighbour (the dealer swaps with the stock). If you hold a King you can reveal it to refuse an incoming swap. Once everyone has acted, the holder of the lowest card loses a life (ties lose one each); at zero lives you are eliminated. The last player standing wins. Simple yet tense, mixing nerve, reading opponents, and a dash of luck.
blurb.cucumber: Suits are irrelevant: beat the highest card played, or dump your lowest.
blurb.curdsandwhey: Thirteen open columns; build down in suit, or park a card on its own rank.
blurb.daifugo: The Japanese 'great rich-man'. Revolutions and suit-locks flip the table — pure rush.
blurb.desmoche: A Nicaraguan rummy dealt nine. Going out takes exactly ten cards, not the nine you were dealt.
blurb.deuceswild: Video Poker with deuces wild. Easier to land hands; great for beginners.
blurb.deucetoseven: Triple-draw lowball where the Ace stays high and straights hurt. The nuts is 7-5-4-3-2 — a WSOP connoisseur's game.
blurb.diplomat: A Forty Thieves relative dealing 104 cards into eight columns of four. The tableau builds down ignoring suit, which makes it the gentle one.
blurb.doppelkopf: A German classic for four in partnerships. The two players holding both ♣Q form 'Re', the rest 'Kontra' — but the teams stay hidden at the start. Fight for 240 points with a unique trump order topped by the ♥10 (Dulle).
blurb.doubleattack: Blackjack where you raise after seeing the dealer’s up-card, on a deck with no tens.
blurb.doubleklondike: Klondike played with two decks of 104 cards. Nine tableau columns and eight foundations (two per suit), with a three-card draw from the stock. Build the tableau down in alternating colours and the foundations up by suit from Ace to King; move all 104 cards to the foundations to win. The doubled deck rewards long look-ahead to avoid dead ends.
blurb.doubt: Doubt (BS). A bluffing duel built for laughter on a relaxed evening.
blurb.doudizhu: China's #1 card game. Bid to become the Landlord and shed your 20 cards before the Peasants team up against you.
blurb.dragontiger: Two cards compared — a baccarat simplification, hugely popular in Asia. For vibe over depth.
blurb.dramaha: Five hole cards that play twice. One draw after the flop, then the pot always splits between an Omaha hand (2 hole + 3 board) and a draw hand made of those same five cards.
blurb.duchess: You choose the rank the foundations start from: pick one of four fans, then build round from King to Ace.
blurb.durak: Russia's attack-defend system, one-of-a-kind. Last one with cards is the 'fool'.
blurb.easthaven: Klondike meets Spider: alternating-color tableau, but the stock deals to every column at once.
blurb.ecarte: A 2-player French trick game played with a 32-card deck, 5 cards each. Before play, an Exchange phase lets the elder (non-dealer) Propose or Stand; if proposed, the dealer Accepts or Refuses; on accept, each player discards any number of cards and draws replacements, repeating until the stock empties. Then 5 strict must-follow tricks are played (rank K>Q>J>A>10>9>8>7). Winning 3+ tricks scores 1 point, all 5 (Vole) scores 2; holding the King of trump scores +1, a turned King gives the dealer +1, and a dealer who refuses then loses gives the elder +1. The first player to reach the target (default 5) wins.
blurb.egyptianratscrew: Slap on doubles or sandwiches. The Slap Jack evolution — reflexes matter.
blurb.eightoff: FreeCell with eight free cells. A gentler cousin; dead ends still possible.
blurb.escoba: A Spanish fishing game of arithmetic: capture table cards that sum to exactly 15 with a hand card. Four players, every one for themselves — clear the table for an Escoba.
blurb.estimation: Call your tricks exactly, for four. A Dash Call (0) and Risk (the highest call) change the size of the swing.
blurb.euchre: Five-card trick-taking with trumps. America's Midwest staple — tight, smart, fast.
blurb.faro: A pure player-vs-bank wagering game that swept American saloons in the 19th century, played with a 52-card deck on a 13-rank (A–K) layout. You first place chips on any ranks; toggle "copper" to bet a rank to lose instead of win. The bank burns the first card (the soda), then deals turns of two cards. Bets on the rank of the first card (the loser) are collected by the bank; bets on the rank of the second card (the winner) are paid 1:1. When both cards match (a split) the bank takes half. The final three cards can be "called" by predicting their order, paying 4:1 for a correct call. Play continues until you run out of chips. Simple to play yet rich with the house edge and the all-or-nothing thrill of the call.
blurb.fiftyone: Manage the running sum so it doesn't exceed 51. A reading-and-rationing curiosity.
blurb.fivecardstud: One down, four up — poker's oldest stud. Simple to learn, deep to read.
blurb.fivehundred: Australia's national trick-taker. Bid for trump and a trick target, with the joker and the two jacks (bowers) ranking highest, in a 4-player partnership game.
blurb.flowergarden: Six open flower-bed fans of six cards plus a sixteen-card bouquet reserve. Pack the beds down by rank with suit ignored, and build foundations up by suit from Ace — a wide-open packer with no stock.
blurb.followthequeen: Every face-up Queen makes the next card's rank wild for everyone. Stud with the ceiling taken off.
blurb.fortress: All 52 cards face-up in 10 columns, building by suit in either direction.
blurb.fortyandeight: Two-deck Forty Thieves variant: 8 columns of 5, with one merciful redeal of the waste.
blurb.fortyfives: An Irish/Canadian 2-team bidding trick-taker. Four players (seats 0&2 vs 1&3) each get 5 cards and play 5 tricks. Bid Pass / 15 / 20 / 25 (Jink); the highest bidder's team declares trump. Fixed top trumps (trump 5 > trump J > ♥A > trump A …) reign, and the top three may be held back instead of following (Reneging). Each trick is worth 5 points: the bidding team scores its points on a make and loses its bid on a miss, while the non-bidding team always scores. First team to the target points (default 45) wins; a 25 Jink (all five tricks) wins instantly.
blurb.fortythieves: Two-deck Forty Thieves. Low completion rate — the austere classic.
blurb.fourcardpoker: Four-card poker vs dealer, with player/dealer betting flexibility.
blurb.fourseasons: A cross and four corners. The foundations start at whatever rank was dealt, and King loops back to Ace.
blurb.fourteenout: Pair exposed column tails that add to 14; K needs an A, and only 7+7 matches in rank.
blurb.freebet: The house pays for your doubles and splits. The price: a dealer 22 pushes.
blurb.freecell: Every card visible — pure strategy. Solve rate scales with skill.
blurb.frenchtarot: A 4-player trick-taker on the full 78-card tarot deck (four 14-card suits with V/C/D/R courts, 21 numbered trumps, and the Excuse). You are seat 0. In the auction each player passes or bids Petite, Garde, Garde Sans, or Garde Contre; the highest bidder becomes the declarer against three CPU defenders. On Petite/Garde the 6-card chien is revealed, merged into the declarer's hand, and six cards are buried (the écart — never Kings or the Excuse). Play follows suit, then trump, with the highest trump winning. The declarer must reach a card-point target that slides with the number of bouts held (trumps 1 and 21, and the Excuse). The deal is scored with a multiplier (Petite ×1 up to Garde Contre ×6), and the highest cumulative score after the set deals wins.
blurb.gaigel: A Swabian 48-card double-deck game in the Schnapsen family. Play in 2 teams, declare King+Queen marriages for bonus points, and race to 101.
blurb.ganjifa: A 3-player Mughal-era Indian trick-taker on a circular 96-card deck of 8 suits x 12 ranks. Each player is dealt 32 cards and 32 tricks are played per round. There is no bidding — trump is auto-declared each round as the dealer's longest suit. The heart of the game is that **the rank order inverts between suit groups**: in a strong suit (design 1-4) higher numbers are stronger and the 12 is the best card, while in a weak suit (design 5-8) lower numbers are stronger and the 1 is. The same "3" is third-from-bottom in a strong suit and third-from-top in a weak one, so comparing raw values gives the opposite answer across half the deck. You must follow the led suit; highest trump wins, else the strongest card of the led suit — "strongest" always meaning the group-aware order. Each trick is one point, and after the configured rounds (3 by default) the highest total wins; a tie leaves no winner.
blurb.gaps: Slide gaps into order. The structural-puzzle feel is unique among solitaires.
blurb.germanwhist: Only the last 13 of 26 tricks score. In the first half, losing on purpose is correct whenever the face-up card is not worth having.
blurb.ginrummy: The two-player Rummy benchmark. Building plus reading the discard pile.
blurb.gofish: Go Fish. 'Got any sevens?' — for relaxed, easy company.
blurb.golf: Golf solitaire. Strip the layout one card at a time — TriPeaks' twin classic.
blurb.gongzhu: Chinese Hearts: the ♠Q (pig) is -100, the ♦J (sheep) +100, and the ♣10 doubles your score. Exposure doubles again.
blurb.goofspiel: Everyone bids face down for the same prize; the highest bid takes it.
blurb.gostop: The Korean sibling of Koi-Koi, a two-player capture game on the same 48-card hanafuda deck. Each player is dealt ten cards with eight face-up on the field. Play a hand card to capture a field card of the same month, then draw from the stock which may also capture. Captured cards score in five Korean categories: Gwang (brights), Godori (the five-bird set), Tti (ribbons), Yeol (animals), and Pi (junk). When you reach the target score you choose go (continue, raising the multiplier) or stop (bank the points). Calling go risks the gwang-bak, pi-bak, and go-bak penalties that double the loss if your opponent turns the tables. First player to the target score wins.
blurb.grandfathersclock: A clock-shaped solitaire: finish each of the twelve faces on the rank of the hour it sits at. No stock, everything visible.
blurb.guandan: A two-pack climbing game from Jiangsu. Four players in two partnerships, 27 cards each; the first side to climb from 2 to the ace wins.
blurb.guts: Guts. A fast pot-vying gamble: everyone is dealt 2 cards and simultaneously declares In (stay) or Out (fold). The players who stayed reveal their hands and the best hand takes the pot — but every other player who stayed must match the pot for the next round, so the pot can snowball. If nobody stays, the pot carries over. Pure nerve and odds.
blurb.hachihachi: The classic three-player Japanese hanafuda game on a 48-card flower deck. Each player is dealt seven cards with six face-up on the field. On your turn you play a hand card to capture a field card of the same month (flower), then draw one card from the stock which may also capture. Unlike Koi-Koi there is no koi-koi/stop decision — when every hand is exhausted the round ends. Captured piles are scored by card points (Bright 20 / Animal 10 / Ribbon 5 / Chaff 1) plus yaku bonuses such as the Five/Three Brights, Boar-Deer-Butterfly, and Red/Blue Ribbons, and each player settles against the 88 baseline (the 264 total card points divided among three players). After the set number of rounds, the highest cumulative score wins.
blurb.handandfoot: A Canasta variant with a hand and a foot. Build red and black canastas to go out as a team.
blurb.hasenpfeffer: A euchre variant from German-American country. The joker is the highest trump of all.
blurb.hearts: Avoid the hearts (and especially the Queen of Spades). The trick-taking benchmark.
blurb.highcardflush: Score by flush length. Simple but with hidden depth — a casino niche worth knowing.
blurb.hokm: Iran's 2v2. The thirteen tricks are never played out — the first partnership to seven takes the hand.
blurb.holdem: Texas Hold'em. The world's most-played poker, for long-game reading nights.
blurb.honeymoonbridge: Bridge for two. The first 13 tricks score nothing -- each one just draws you a card.
blurb.horse: Five poker disciplines rotating at one table. The chips carry over; only the rules change every few hands.
blurb.indianpoker: You can't see your own card — only your opponent's reactions. Best with close friends.
blurb.indianrummy: India's 13-card Rummy for 2-4 players. Two decks plus jokers; form valid melds of 2+ sequences, at least one pure (joker-free). The turned-up wild joker rank is the key twist.
blurb.irishpoker: Four hole cards, discard two after the flop. A volatile Hold'em hybrid.
blurb.ironcross: Five community cards in a cross, but only the vertical or the horizontal three play. The centre is the one card both arms share.
blurb.israeliwhist: Bidding twice: an auction for trump and a quota, then everyone calls their own target separately.
blurb.jass: Switzerland's national card game. The Schieber variant lets you pass the trump bid to your partner — a uniquely Swiss twist.
blurb.jokerpoker: Video Poker with a joker. The wild-card moment changes everything.
blurb.schafkopf: Bavaria's national trick-taking game. Thirty-two cards deal out to four players, and the declarer picks one of **three contracts**: Rufspiel (call a fail ace to gain a hidden partner), Wenz (only the Unters are trump) or Solo (a chosen suit plus the Obers and Unters, played alone). The contract *is* the trump structure, so the same hand changes rank order depending on what gets declared. The declaring side needs 61 of the 120 points.
blurb.julepe: A Spanish Rams-family betting trick-taker for three to five players. Everyone antes, then chooses to enter or drop. **The required trick count scales with how many stay in** (the five tricks divided among the entrants, rounded up), and an entrant who falls short pays into the pot *and* has their ante doubled next hand — the "beast". Dropping costs only the ante.
blurb.kaiser: The Canadian partnership bidding game. The five of hearts is worth +5 and the three of spades -3, together weighing as much as all eight tricks.
blurb.kalooki: Two-deck Rummy with jokers. Open with 51+ points; jokers are wild.
blurb.karnoffel: The oldest card game known by name, attested in 1426. Five cards each from a 48-card pack with the aces removed, and the lowest of four face-up cards picks the trump suit.
blurb.unsunkaruta: Unsun Karuta is the oldest surviving Japanese trick-taking game, still played in Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto. Seventy-five cards in **five** suits of fifteen, eight players in two teams of four. **The pip order flips with the suit** — nine is highest in the long suits (Pao, Isu), **one is highest in the round suits** (Kotsu, Oru and the fifth suit Kuru). And **following suit is not automatic**: only when the leader declares (meri or monchi) must everyone follow.
blurb.quodlibet: Quodlibet is the Austrian students' **compendium trick-taker**: 32 cards, eight each to four players, and **twelve deals arranged as three "wheels" of four contracts**. The dealer may only pick from **the wheel currently in play**. **Every score is a penalty and the fewest wins** — so a contract you want to win tricks in (Plus) sits at the same table as ones you want to duck (Minus, Bad Neighbour). In the third wheel **what you can see becomes the rule**: under Open Trousers your own hand is the one you cannot see, and under Good Hunting every hand is face up.
blurb.dehlapakad: Dehla Pakad means **"catch the tens"** — an Indian partnership trick-taker where the hand is decided by **how many of the four tens you take**, not by tricks. But the heart of it is elsewhere: **winning a trick does not give you its cards.** They pile up in the centre and are only gathered in when **the same player wins two tricks in a row**. A ten can be won three times over and still belong to nobody, so the question at every trick is never "can I take it" but "**can I take this one and the next**". The judgement is asymmetric too: the non-dealer's side wins with two tens, the dealer's side needs three.
blurb.sutda: Sutda (섯다) is the Korean betting game on a **20-card hanafuda pack — months 1 to 10, two of each**. Your hand is just **two cards**, and you bet on what they make. **Only months 1, 3 and 8 hold a *gwang* (bright)**: hanafuda's brights are months 1, 3, 8, 11 and 12, and 11-12 are not in a 1-10 pack — which is exactly why there are **only three gwang-ttaeng, 38 > 18 > 13**. Below them come the ttaeng (same-month pairs), then named pairs like ali, doksa and seryuk, then *kkeut*: the last digit of the two months added. **The weakest named pair still beats the strongest kkeut** — that is the hinge of the whole ranking.
blurb.cirulla: Cirulla is the Ligurian **fishing** game on Scopa's 40-card pack, with **one more way to capture**: alongside matching a single card and taking a set that sums to the card you played, you may take a set whose total **plus your card makes fifteen**. Fifteen is added, not substituted — taking a seven with a seven still works. And an **ace played to a table with no ace on it sweeps everything**. Every deal of three carries a bonus: 3 points if they total nine or less, 10 for three of a kind, with the **seven of hearts wild for the bonus only**.
blurb.diloti: Diloti is a Greek **fishing** game, and its name is the Greek verb δηλώνω, "to declare": you bundle your played card with loose table cards and **declare a value of 2-10**, building a pile only that value can take. Captures do **not** sum to ten - they sum to **the played card's own rank**, so a 5 takes 2+3, and several disjoint sets at once. **Face cards take exactly one** match, never join a sum, and cannot be laid off while their match sits on the table. And a **one-card sweep of the whole table - a xeri (ξερή) - scores 10**, against just eleven fixed points a round, so it usually decides the round.
blurb.comet: Comet is the 17th-century French ancestor of the **stops** family, named after Halley's Comet in 1682. Sequences climb **by rank and ignore suit entirely** - ♠5 → ♥6 → ♠7 is normal, and that is precisely what separates it from same-suit Michigan. The **9 of diamonds is the Comet**, standing in for any rank; playing it stops the sequence and lets you lead the next one, but being **left holding it costs a point**. The pack is the standard 52 **with the 8 of diamonds removed**, and whatever will not deal evenly is buried face down - those two are where runs reliably stop, which is what the family is named for.
blurb.costlycolours: Costly Colours is a 17th-century Shropshire game for two and an **ancestor of Cribbage** - and the missing crib is the least of the differences. The deal is **three cards each**, the next is **turned up for trumps** (a turned Jack pegs the dealer 4), and before play each side may **exchange one card** - **refusing pegs 1 for the opponent**. The count scores at **15, 25 and 31** (**the 25 has no counterpart in Cribbage**), a prial scores **9** and a double prial **18**. The show is not fifteens but a **ladder of colours**, topped by **four in suit for 6** - the "Costly Colours" the game is named for.
blurb.kemps: A 4-player, 2-team matching game built on secret signals. Each turn you swap one of your four cards for a card on the shared field, racing to collect four of a kind. When your partner gets four of a kind they flash the secret signal you agreed on (Sound or Blink), and your team shouts "Kemps!" for a point — but if the opposing team spots the signal first they call "Counter-Kemps!" and steal it. First team to 5 points wins. A game of bluff, observation, and teamwork.
blurb.kille: The Swedish Cuckoo game on its own 42-card pack. You hold a single card and trade with your neighbour to avoid ending up lowest.
blurb.king: A four-player compendium of trick-avoidance games on a standard 52-card deck. Each match is exactly seven deals, and the rotating dealer picks one of seven unused contracts (No Tricks, No Hearts, No Queens, No King of Hearts, No Last Two, No Men, or King with a chosen trump). Play thirteen must-follow tricks and try to dodge the penalty cards the current contract punishes — the highest total (fewest penalties) after all seven deals wins.
blurb.kingalbert: Nine open columns plus a seven-card reserve. Alternating-color packing with no way back into the reserve — every reserve card is a one-shot.
blurb.kingo: The same kabufuda deck as Oicho-Kabu, but you collect matching numbers instead of chasing a total.
blurb.klaberjass: The two-player ancestor of Belote and Pinochle. In trumps the jack scores 20 and the nine 14, both outranking the ace.
blurb.klaverjas: The national trick-taker of the Netherlands. Four players (2 vs 2) play a 32-card deck with must-follow play and forced overtrumping. The trump Jack (20) and Nine (14) rule, and runs and marriages earn Roem (bonus). Partner up and battle over card points plus Roem in this deep, demanding game.
blurb.klondike: The Windows solitaire we all know. The long road to completion is good for the soul.
blurb.knockoutwhist: A British survival trick-taker for 4 players on a 52-card deck. Round 1 deals 7 cards, and each round deals one fewer. The previous round's winner's longest suit becomes trump (auto); play is must-follow, ace high. A player who wins zero tricks in a round must spend a Dogbone token (each starts with 1) to survive — and is knocked out once the Dogbones run out. The last player standing wins this tense, ever-shrinking elimination game.
blurb.koenigrufen: An Austrian 4-player tarock game on the 54-card tarock deck (four 8-card suits with J/C/Q/K courts, 21 numbered trumps, and the Sküs). You are seat 0. The declarer who wins the Rufer (King-calling) auction calls a King, and whoever holds it becomes a secret partner (their identity stays hidden until that King is first played). The declarer merges the 6-card talon into hand and buries six (never Kings or the Trull honours — trumps 1, 21, and the Sküs), then partners up against the other two. Play follows suit, then trump, with the highest trump winning. The declaring team wins the deal by capturing enough card-points across the tricks. The highest cumulative score after the set number of deals wins.
blurb.koikoi: A two-player Japanese hanafuda matching (capture) game on a 48-card flower deck. Each player is dealt eight cards with eight face-up on the field. On your turn you play a hand card to capture a field card of the same month (flower), then draw one card from the stock which may also capture. Captured cards form 'yaku' (combinations) such as the Five/Three Brights, Boar-Deer-Butterfly, Red and Blue Ribbons, Animals, Ribbons, Chaff, and the Flower/Moon Viewing sake sets. Whenever you complete a yaku you choose koi-koi (continue to build a bigger score, raising the multiplier) or shobu (stop and bank the points) — but calling koi-koi risks your opponent completing a yaku first. First player to the target score wins.
blurb.labellelucie: A classic French fan solitaire. 52 cards are dealt into 17 fans of three; only each fan's top card moves, building down in suit onto another fan or up from the Ace on four foundations. When stuck, gather the remaining cards, shuffle and redeal — but only three times. Run out of redeals while stuck and you lose.
blurb.laughandliedown: A five-handed English fishing game from the 1600s: take one or three of a rank from twelve face-up cards, or lay your whole hand down and go out.
blurb.letitride: One decision: pull back your bet or let it ride. The simplest rules, the purest tension.
blurb.lingerlonger: Win a trick, draw a card. The last player still holding cards wins.
blurb.literature: A deduction fishing game from India and Canada. Six players in two teams of three share a 48-card pack with the eights removed, contesting eight half-suits. Even a teammate’s hand is hidden.
blurb.loba: An Argentine rummy on 108 cards. A set needs three DIFFERENT suits, and jokers go only into runs.
blurb.loo: A pot-based gambling trick-taker that swept 18th-19th-century England. Four players (you + 3 CPU) each get five cards on a 52-card deck, and the turn-up card sets trump. Everyone antes into a carried-over pot, then decides to play or pass on the strength of their hand. Participants fight five must-follow / must-head tricks (you must beat the current winner when you can), each trick winning one-fifth of the pot. A participant who takes no trick is 'looed' and pays a penalty into the next deal's pot. There is no target score, so it is a repeating deal loop where you build up chips.
blurb.macau: A European Crazy Eights with magic cards. Stack 2s to pile on draw penalties, skip with 7s, reverse with Jacks — and shout "Macau!" on your last card.
blurb.machiavelli: Italy's Rummikub-with-cards. 2-5 players share a single table of melds you may freely rearrange; using two 52-card decks (104 cards), the first to empty their hand wins. Rebuilding existing melds is the heart of the game.
blurb.madrasso: The most popular card game of the Veneto: a four-player partnership trick-taker on the Italian 40-card pack, ten cards each, where **the suit of the last card dealt becomes trump**. Trumps beat any plain card and following suit is otherwise mandatory. The rank order A>3>K>Q>J>7..2 matches the point values (A=11, 3=10, K=4, Q=3, J=2), so the most valuable card is also the strongest. Taking the majority of the card points wins the deal.
blurb.manille: A traditional French/Belgian trump trick-taker. Four players (2 vs 2) play a 32-card deck where the 10 (Manille) is the strongest card and the Ace (Manillon) is second. Trump is the suit of the last dealt card; must-follow play forces you to trump unless your partner already holds the trick. No declarations — just chase card points with your partner.
blurb.mao: The legendary party game of Crazy Eights plus a secret hidden rule. Nobody tells you the rule; break it and you draw a penalty with no explanation. Comply 3 times and a vague hint finally unlocks.
blurb.marias: The national trick-taker of Czechia and Slovakia. Three players battle over a 32-card deck where one rotating Soloist plays alone against the 2 Defenders. Trump is the Soloist's longest suit (auto); rank runs A>10>K>Q>J>9>8>7, and a King+Queen of one suit scores a marriage (20, or 40 if trump). The final-trick +10 bonus and the doubled Defender scores on a Soloist loss keep every hand tense.
blurb.memory: The matching game. Memory training across generations.
blurb.mendikot: India's 2v2. Neither points nor tricks decide it -- the four tens do.
blurb.michigan: Michigan (Newmarket). A 'stops' chip-betting family game. Players first stake chips across four center 'boodle' cards (A♥, K♣, Q♦, J♠), then play cards in ascending same-suit sequences. A 'stop' occurs when the next card sits in the face-down dead hand or the run passes the King, and the last player to play starts a fresh sequence. Playing a card that matches a boodle wins its chips; the first player to empty their hand ends the round. After the set number of rounds the richest player wins — a light, luck-and-timing family classic.
blurb.mighty: Korea's take on Napoleon. The Spade Ace ('Mighty') sits at the center of the bidding.
blurb.minchiate: A 16th-century Florentine 97-card tarot trick-taker for 4 in fixed 2v2 teams (opposite seats partner), with no bidding. The deck is 4 suits x 14 = 56 + 40 trumps + the Matto. **The 40-trump ladder is the longest in this collection** and is not a plain number line -- its upper reaches carry the 12 zodiac signs, the four elements and the virtues -- so trumps are shown by name (Angelo, Eremita, Stella, ...) rather than by number, because a bare number tells you nothing beyond "is 35 stronger than 36". 97 does not divide by 4, so each player gets 21 and the dealer takes the remaining 13 and buries them (scarto); buried cards score for the dealer's team, which is why trumps and the Matto cannot be discarded. You must follow the led suit and must trump when void; the Matto alone is exempt and never takes a trick. **A led Matto does not set the led suit** -- the next non-Matto card does. Scoring is one point per trick plus a last-trick bonus and the 13 buried cards, and after the configured rounds (default 4) the higher team total wins; a tie leaves no winner.
blurb.minibridge: Bridge without the auction: everyone announces their HCP and the stronger pair declares.
blurb.mississippistud: Build five cards with raise decisions all along the way. Fast tempo, deep reading.
blurb.missmilligan: A hard two-deck solitaire: when you run dry, deal eight more at once — one onto every column.
blurb.montebank: Suit is all that matters. Back a lone suit and it's even; back a duplicate and it bleeds.
blurb.montecarlo: Adjacent-pair removal. Pyramid's cousin, more luck-tinged.
blurb.mrsmop: Spider with nothing hidden: 104 cards into 13 columns, all face up, no stock.
blurb.mus: A Basque vying game for four (2 vs 2). Across four rounds — Grande, Chica, Pares, Juego — bluff and trade cards to win amarrakos without showing your hand, with an Órdago all-in for a sudden-death swing.
blurb.mushi: An Osaka hanafuda game on 40 cards -- June and July are out -- where the willow lightning card is wild and takes any card you like.
blurb.nainjaune: The French stops game. The run never looks at suit -- it climbs by rank and ends on a king.
blurb.nap: A British classic gambling trick-taker with a bidding phase. Four players are dealt 5 cards each and bid once — Pass / Two (2 tricks) / Three (3 tricks) / Four (4 tricks) / Nap (all 5 tricks, high stakes). The highest bidder becomes the declarer who picks trump and leads; play is must-follow, ace high. Make the contract to win chips (a successful Nap wins 10); miss it and the opponents each win the bid value (a failed Nap costs 5 each). First to the target chips (default 20) wins.
blurb.napoleon: A Japan-born bidding game. The 'Napoleon' and 'aide' interplay is uniquely charming.
blurb.napoleonssquare: A large two-deck solitaire laid out as a square; same-suit runs move as one unit.
blurb.narcotic: Four piles; discard all four exposed cards when their ranks match. Redeals are unlimited.
blurb.nertz: Simultaneous-solitaire multiplayer combat. Hands and brain both stay very busy.
blurb.ninetynine: Bury 3 cards to set your secret bid, then hit it exactly. A clever twist on trick-taking.
blurb.niuniu: A Chinese banking game: find three of your five cards summing to a multiple of ten, and the remaining pair's last digit is your hand.
blurb.oasispoker: Caribbean Stud plus one card-swap. The extra decision opens it up for strategy-minded players.
blurb.ohhell: Bid the exact tricks you'll win. The bidding/luck balance is exquisite.
blurb.oichokabu: Japan's kabufuda baccarat: chase a 9, dodge a 0. Draw a third card or stand against the banker.
blurb.oldmaid: The 'Old Maid'. Every Japanese kid knows this one; losing well is half the fun.
blurb.omaha: Four hole cards, use two — heavyweight poker. Hand combinations multiply; your brain warms up.
blurb.omahahilo: Omaha with hi/lo split. Thinking in two directions per hand — for poker veterans.
blurb.ombre: The classic Spanish soloist-vs-coalition trick-taker that swept 17th-century Europe, played by three on a 40-card Spanish deck (no 8/9/10). A bid phase (pass / entrar / solo) plus a chosen trump suit decides the Ombre, who plays alone against the coalition of the other two over nine tricks. The trump group ranks Spadille (♠A) > Manille (7 of trump) > Basto (♣A) > Punto (Ace of trump, red only) > K > Q > J > 6..2. Sacar (Ombre takes the most tricks) scores; Puesta (a tie) penalizes the Ombre; Codille (an opponent wins) doubles it. Highest cumulative score after the set deals wins.
blurb.openfacechinese: A patience-meets-poker game for 2 to 4 players against the CPU, played with a standard 52-card deck. Cards are dealt one at a time and each must be committed immediately to one of three rows — Top (3 cards), Middle (5 cards) or Bottom (5 cards) — and once placed a card can never be moved. Your rows must rank in non-decreasing strength from Top to Bottom; break that order and you foul, scoring nothing for the round. Strong rows in the right spot earn royalty bonuses, and a premium Top row (a pair of Queens or better) sends you to Fantasyland. Each round your rows are compared row-by-row against the other players, scoring points for every row you win plus royalties, and the highest cumulative total after the target number of rounds takes the game. The tension comes from committing cards blind, with no way to undo a misplacement.
blurb.osmosis: An unusual logic puzzle where ranks seep from upper rows to lower ones. For players tired of building sequences.
blurb.pageone: Japan's UNO-like. Every household has its own house rules — and nostalgia.
blurb.paigow: Seven cards, two hands — Asian-flavored casino. Plenty of time to think. For nights where thought beats tempo.
blurb.pan: Panguingue (Pan). A large multi-deck rummy from the saloons of Mexico and the American Southwest. It uses eight 40-card decks (the 8s, 9s and 10s removed — 320 cards in all) dealt ten to a hand across 3-6 players. On your turn draw from the stock or discard, lay down sets and ropes (runs — since 8/9/10 are gone, 7 is followed by J), lay single cards off onto existing melds, then discard to end your turn. Qualifying melds are automatically paid in chips by the other players, and the first to meld eleven cards declares 'Pan' and wins — a classic rummy with a distinctive casino chip economy.
blurb.pasur: Iran's fishing game: capture to eleven, and emptying the table doubles what you took.
blurb.penguin: Dynamic base rank FreeCell variant. Same-suit descending with wraparound.
blurb.perseverance: Twelve columns, aces already up; build down in suit and move whole runs at once.
blurb.pig: Collect four of a kind, then quietly touch your nose. Last to notice takes a letter.
blurb.pigstail: Pig's Tail. Snatch matching cards from the table; the laughter is inevitable.
blurb.pineapple: Hold'em with three hole cards (discard one). Extra reading material per hand.
blurb.pinochle: A classic American household game with a custom deck. Melds and trumps for mid-level players.
blurb.piquet: A 17th-century two-player French classic — perhaps the oldest trick-taking on record.
blurb.pishti: A Turkish capture (fishing) card game for 2–4 players on a standard 52-card deck. Each player is dealt 4 cards and plays one onto a central pile in turn. Playing a card that matches the rank of the pile's top card — or playing a Jack, which is wild and captures anything — sweeps the entire pile. Capturing a lone card on the pile scores a Pişti (+10 points; +20 for a Jack played onto a single Jack). Hands are re-dealt 4 at a time until the stock runs out. Final scoring: most cards +3, each Ace +1, 2♣ +2, 10♦ +3, each Jack +1, plus Pişti bonuses. The highest total wins.
blurb.pitch: American Southern trick-taking. Bidding intensity for those in the know.
blurb.poch: A 15th-century German game in three stages. Chips go onto a nine-pool board and are claimed with cards of the turn-up's suit.
blurb.poker: Classic five-card draw. The original tell-reading poker, against the CPU as long as you'd like.
blurb.pokersquares: Place into a 5x5 grid to form poker hands. A placement puzzle for poker brains.
blurb.polignac: Only the four jacks cost you anything — and the jack of spades (the Polignac) costs double. You may also declare capot and go for every trick.
blurb.pontoon: British blackjack, where every hand is dealt face down — the banker's included, so there is no up-card to read.
blurb.popejoan: The ancestor of the stops family. The eight of diamonds is out of the pack, so a run always dies at the seven.
blurb.preference: A Russian/Austrian classic trick-taker with a bidding phase. Three players each get 10 cards from a 32-card deck and fight over 10 tricks. Each bids once — Pass / Six (6 tricks) / Misère (0 tricks, no trump) / Seven (7 tricks) / Eight (8 tricks), ranking Pass < Six < Misère < Seven < Eight. The highest bidder becomes the declarer who plays alone against the other 2 defenders; trump is the declarer's longest suit (auto), and Misère has no trump. Play is must-follow, ace high. Make the contract and the declarer scores its value (Six=6 / Seven=7 / Eight=8 / Misère=10); miss it and each defender scores the same. An all-pass round is void. First to the target points (default 30) wins.
blurb.president: The English-speaking world's Daifugo. Comparing house rules is half the fun.
blurb.primero: Primero. A Renaissance (16th-century) vying pot game and one of the oldest ancestors of poker — famously played at the Tudor court. Each player antes and is dealt 4 cards, then takes turns to call, raise (vie), or fold. When betting closes the non-folded players reveal their hands, which rank from Numerus up through Primero (one card of each suit), Supremus, and Fluxus (four of a suit); the best hand takes the pot. Pure bluff and nerve, with no shared cards.
blurb.prsi: Czech Crazy Eights with a 32-card deck. Match the discard top by suit or rank; 7s stack a draw-two penalty, Aces and Unders (Jacks) skip the next player. No wild card — first to empty their hand wins outright.
blurb.put: Three cards, three tricks — the 3 is the strongest card and the 4 the weakest. Say “Put” at any time to double the stake in this old English game of nerve.
blurb.pyramid: Match to thirteen. Short rounds; a luck-tinged breather.
blurb.quadrille: An 18th-century French four-player expansion of Ombre. All 40 cards are dealt, ten each, and the winning bidder — the Quadrille — calls the King of a suit they do not hold; whoever holds it becomes a temporary partner. The called suit is public, but the holder stays hidden until that King is played. Trump ranking is Spadille (♠A) > Manille (the 7 of trump) > Basto (♣A). Holding all four Kings means playing alone (Roi seul).
blurb.germansolo: The German branch of the Ombre-to-Quadrille line. Thirty-two cards, eight each, and three fixed matadors that outrank every other trump whatever trumps are: **Spadille (Q of clubs), Manille (the 7 of trumps) and Basta (Q of spades)**. The auction climbs Frage (call an ace you do not hold and its holder becomes a **hidden partner**; five tricks) to Solo (five tricks alone) to Tout (**all eight**, alone). If everyone passes, whoever holds Spadille is forced to play the Mussfrage.
blurb.gleek: A three-hander from Tudor England where **points move four separate times in a single deal**. First the stock is auctioned (the eldest hand must open at 12 and may not pass), and the buyer pays half the bid to each opponent before swapping seven cards. Then the **ruff** (best single-suit total takes it — four aces beat any ruff whatsoever), then **gleeks and mournivals** (three and four of a rank), and finally twelve tricks in which the trump honours carry outsized values: Tib is worth 15, Tom 9.
blurb.rams: A pot game for three to five. Choose to play or drop — and playing without taking a single trick costs you extra.
blurb.ramsch: Skat turned inside out: whoever takes the most card points loses them. Three players, jacks always trump, no auction.
blurb.rankandfile: Ten columns of four, three hidden; build down in alternating colour and move any sequence.
blurb.razz: Seven-card lowball. The low hand wins — a mental flip that connoisseurs adore.
blurb.reddog: Will a third card fall between two? The fastest cycle on the floor.
blurb.reversis: Avoidance on a 48-card pack with the 10s removed. The Quinola (J♥) and the A♦ cost you points *and* chips. Fewest penalties takes the pool.
blurb.rikken: A Dutch auction where "take eight" and "take none" sit on the same ladder.
blurb.ristikontra: Match the previous card's rank to sweep the pile — and if someone sweeps, laying that same rank steals it right back. A Finnish 2-vs-2 capture game.
blurb.rollingstone: Tricks are worth nothing; failing to follow suit hands you the whole pile.
blurb.rook: An American 4-player, 2-team point-trick game played not with a French deck but a special 57-card deck (four colors — red, gold, green, black — numbered 1–14, plus the Rook bird). An auction sets a points contract (70–120); the winning bidder takes the 5-card nest into hand, discards 5, and declares a trump color. Point cards (5 = 5, 10 & 14 = 10 each, 1 = 15, Rook bird = 20) are captured in tricks by each team. The declaring team scores if it makes its bid and loses points otherwise. The first team to 500 points wins.
blurb.royalcotillion: Foundations climb by twos and wrap — after the King comes the deuce — so eight piles swallow all 104 cards.
blurb.rummy500: Race to 500. American household Rummy in its mid-form classic shape.
blurb.russianbank: A two-deck head-to-head solitaire against the CPU. Each player races to empty their 13-card reserve onto 8 shared foundations (A→K by suit) and 4 shared tableau columns (alternating colour, descending). Out of moves? Discard a hand card to pass the turn. Catch the CPU leaving a forced move with "Stop!" to seize tempo.
blurb.russianpoker: Oasis Poker evolved. Buy a 6th card, force dealer exchanges — the most decision-rich casino poker variant.
blurb.russiansolitaire: Yukon, but crueler. Lowest completion rate — for experts only.
blurb.sakura: Kumamoto hanafuda scored by counting, not by yaku. Add up the cards you took: Bright 20, Animal 10, Ribbon 5, Chaff 1.
blurb.saliclaw: A 96-card solitaire with the eight queens removed. Each king dealt opens a new column, and the foundations run ace to jack ignoring suit.
blurb.samba: A three-deck Canasta variant: build same-suit sequences (sambas) alongside sets in 4-player partnerships.
blurb.scarto: A 3-player Italian tarocchi trick-taker on the full 78-card tarot deck (four 14-card suits with V/C/D/R courts, 21 numbered trumps, and the Excuse). You are seat 0. There is no bidding, no chien, and no partnership: the dealer performs the scarto, burying three surplus low pip cards, then the three players play out the tricks. Play follows suit, then trump, with the highest trump winning. Each deal is scored as a zero-sum settlement against the average of the players' captured card-points, and the highest cumulative score after the set deals wins.
blurb.piedmontesetarot: Tarocco Piemontese is the 78-card tarot of Piedmont in northern Italy. Where `scarto` is the **fixed three-player** short form, this is the standard game for **three or four** — nineteen cards each and a two-card talon at four seats. The count differs too: the classic Italian method takes cards **in groups of three, each worth its values minus two**, which comes to exactly 78 points for the deck (kept in thirds so the remainders survive). Honours (trumps 1 and 21, the Matto) and court cards cannot be buried in the dealer's scarto.
blurb.schnapsen: Austria's two-player gem. Marriages, a closing stock, and a tense race to 66.
blurb.scopa: An Italian fishing game: one card captures the table. Chasing the board-clearing 'scopa' is addictive.
blurb.scopone: The 4-player, 2-team version of Scopa. All ten cards are dealt up front — coordinate with your partner to win the board.
blurb.scorpion: Spider-like layout with its own twists. A mid-level diversion.
blurb.seahaventowers: Towers-family. Suit-only stacking — stricter than FreeCell, more austere.
blurb.sedma: A Czech/Slovak no-trump capture trick-taker on a 32-card deck. Four players in two teams play with no follow obligation — any card is legal. A card captures the trick when its rank matches the lead or it is a 7 (wild), and the last to capture wins. Aces and 10s are worth 10 points each, plus +10 for the last trick. The fun is in hoarding your 7s to steal point-rich tricks.
blurb.sergeantmajor: The British army's three-hander. Nobody bids -- the seats owe 8, 5 and 3.
blurb.setteemezzo: The Italian seven-and-a-half. Face cards are worth half a point, so drawing one on seven lands you exactly on target.
blurb.sevenbridge: Japan's household Rummy. Simple rules, surprisingly tense.
blurb.sevencardstud: No community cards — pure classic stud. Read what you can see; love the basics.
blurb.sevencardstudhilo: Split-pot stud: the high and the low share the pot, but if nobody makes an eight-or-better low the high takes it all.
blurb.chicago: Seven-card stud, except **half the pot goes to a single card — the highest spade you hold face-down**. Only the other half is decided by poker hands. Where `sevencardstudhilo` gives that half to the best eight-or-better low, Chicago gives it to one card nobody else can see. No spade in the hole and you cannot win that half; if nobody holds one, the high hand takes everything. The ace of spades is the highest.
blurb.eightgame: Eight-Game Mix rotates **eight disciplines** at one table. It adds No-Limit Hold'em, Pot-Limit Omaha and 2-7 Triple Draw to the five that `horse` already rotates (Limit Hold'em, Omaha Hi-Lo, Razz, Stud, Stud Hi-Lo). Same seats, same chips, changing rules — and unlike H.O.R.S.E., **one of the disciplines asks you to draw**. The match ends when one seat holds every chip.
blurb.sevens: Place cards from a 7. Hold-back tactics produce surprisingly deep reads.
blurb.seventwentyseven: Chase 7 and 27 at the same time. Face cards are half a point, an ace is 1 or 11, and going over kills that side.
blurb.shamrocks: Eighteen fans; stack by rank in either direction, suit ignored, three cards to a fan.
blurb.sheepshead: A Bavarian 5-player trick-taker. The 'picker' takes the blind and calls a suit to bind a hidden partner, then both fight for points around the trump Queens and Jacks. Dense strategy.
blurb.shelem: What is bid is the score itself, not a number of tricks. With a widow exchange and an all-tricks Shelem call.
blurb.shengji: A two-pack point-trick game from China. Four players in two partnerships, 25 cards each, contesting the 200 points in the fives, tens and kings while climbing from 2 to the ace.
blurb.shithead: A three-layer (hand/visible/hidden) discarding game. A favorite in bars worldwide.
blurb.shortdeck: Short deck (no 2-5). Flushes and straights flip in strength; the tempo lifts.
blurb.simplesimon: An easier Spider-family solitaire. All 52 cards are dealt face-up into 10 columns with no stock and no free cells. Move a single top card or a same-suit descending run; a complete King-to-Ace same-suit run is removed automatically. Clear all four suits to win. Because every card is visible, it plays like a look-ahead puzzle.
blurb.sirtommy: One of the oldest recorded patiences: deal the stock into four wastes and build A-K foundations.
blurb.sixbidsolo: A three-hander dealing eleven cards each from a 36-card pack, with three more face down as a widow. Six bids swap the target and the payment together.
blurb.sixcardgolf: A memory & exchange game where you swap face-down cards to get the lowest score
blurb.sjavs: The Faroese national game. Both black queens and all four jacks are trumps whatever the trump suit, played four-handed in fixed partnerships.
blurb.skat: Germany's national bidding masterpiece. One of trick-taking's all-time greats.
blurb.skitgubbe: Two phases, two different games: duel for cards first, then shed the cards you won. The last one holding cards is the dirty old man.
blurb.slapjack: Slap when a Jack appears. Loud-table laughter, guaranteed.
blurb.slobberhannes: Three tricks you must not take: the first, the last, and the one with the Q of clubs. Escape all three and you score. No trump.
blurb.slyfox: A two-deck solitaire dealt into twenty reserve slots, with four foundations building up from the aces and four down from the kings.
blurb.snap: Call it the instant a card matches the one before it, and the whole pile is yours.
blurb.soko: Stud with two extra hands — a four-card straight and a four-card flush. Hands you would fold now play.
blurb.solowhist: A British classic trick-taker with a bidding phase. Four players each bid once — Pass / Solo (win 8 tricks alone) / Misère (win 0 tricks, no trump) / Abundance (win 9 tricks alone). The highest bidder becomes the declarer who plays alone against the other 3 defenders. For Solo and Abundance the declarer's longest suit is trump (auto); play is must-follow, ace high. Make the contract and the declarer scores it; miss it and each defender scores. First to the target points wins.
blurb.somerset: All 52 cards face-up in 10 columns, building down by alternating colour.
blurb.spades: Declare your spade-led tricks. A team game beloved in the English-speaking world.
blurb.spanish21: A BlackJack offshoot using a Spanish deck (no tens). Double-wins and surrender add flair for the casino-fluent.
blurb.speculation: An auction over the best trump. Every new lead invites a rival to buy it off you.
blurb.speed: Speed. The fastest of card reflex games — a round takes seconds.
blurb.spider: A two-deck epic. For nights you want a long, focused sit-down.
blurb.spiderette: Single-deck Spider. The right length for a mid-session focus break.
blurb.spiteandmalice: A two-player deck-clear race. Attack/defense balance for solitaire fans crossing over.
blurb.spoilfive: An Irish classic trick-taker (also called Maw) for 5 players on a 52-card deck, dealing 5 cards each and playing for a pot every round. Trump is the turned-up card; the three top trumps — the trump 5 (highest), the trump J, and the ♥A (always a trump) — outrank everything and may be held back instead of following suit (Reneging). The first player to win 3 of the 5 tricks takes the pot at once; if nobody reaches 3 it is a Spoil and the pot carries over. First player to the target score (30 by default) wins this game of unusual rank order and carried-over stakes.
blurb.spoons: An American 4-player party speed game. From a 52-card deck each player is dealt 4 cards, then everyone continuously passes a single card to the next player. The moment someone collects four of a kind they grab a spoon, and everyone races for the remaining spoons (one fewer than the number of players). Whoever is left without a spoon gains a letter — S, P, O, O, N, S. After six letters that player is eliminated, and the last player standing wins. It is all about reflexes and nerve.
blurb.stalactites: A FreeCell variant whose foundation base rank changes every deal, and suits are ignored.
blurb.stealingbundles: A fishing game where a rival bundle can be taken whole if its top card matches.
blurb.sthelena: A two-deck solitaire with twelve columns circling the foundations — the king row builds down, the ace row up, and the tableau moves by rank alone.
blurb.streetsandalleys: All 52 cards open across eight columns — no reserve, no stock. A pure packer for planners.
blurb.sueca: The national trick-taker of Portugal and Brazil. Four players (2 vs 2) play a 40-card deck with must-follow trump play. There are no declarations at all — just chase the high-value Aces (11) and Sevens (10) and take the majority of the 120 card points with your partner.
blurb.sultan: Two-deck patience around eight King-based foundations and an eight-slot Divan reserve.
blurb.tablanet: A Balkan (Serbian/Macedonian) fishing (capture) game on a 52-card deck. Four players (you + 3 CPU, individual scoring) are each dealt four cards with four face-up on the table. A played number card captures table cards of the same rank and any subset whose values sum to it (multiple groups at once); Queens and Kings capture only by matching rank; a Jack sweeps the whole table except other Jacks. Clearing the table with a single non-Jack card scores a 'Tabla' bonus. Fresh hands are dealt until the stock runs out, and leftover table cards go to the last player who captured. Score the most cards, the 10♦, the 2♣, each Ace, each Jack, and every Tabla — highest total wins.
blurb.tarabish: A 36-card partnership game of the Jass family: in trump the J (Jass) and 9 (Menel) outrank the ace. Runs and bella score as melds.
blurb.tarneeb: A Middle Eastern trump game. Thirteen tricks, four players, simple yet deep.
blurb.tarocchini: A 4-player Bolognese trick-taker in fixed 2v2 teams (opposite seats partner) on the 62-card Tarocco Bolognese deck: 4 suits of 10 (the low pips 2-5 are absent) + 21 trumps + the Matto. There is no bidding. 62 does not divide by 4, so each player gets 15 and the dealer takes the remaining 2 and buries them (scarto); buried cards score for the dealer's team, which is why trumps and the Matto may not be discarded. The heart of the game is that **the four papi rank equal and the later-played one wins the trick**. Every other trick-taker resolves with "the winner changes only on a strictly stronger card", and carrying that instinct over makes you expect the first papa to win. Note they are a middle group: a higher ordinary trump still beats them. You must follow the led suit, and must trump when void; the Matto alone is exempt and never takes a trick. Scoring is one point per trick plus a last-trick bonus and the two buried cards, and after the configured rounds (default 4, constrained to a multiple of the player count) the higher team total wins — a tie leaves no winner.
blurb.teendopaanch: Northern India, three-handed. The seats owe 3, 2 and 5 tricks -- assigned, never bid.
blurb.teenpatti: The Indian variant of Three Card Brag — a 4-player vying game played with a 52-card deck, 3 cards each, plus chips and a pot. Each player is Blind (hasn't looked) or Seen. On your turn: See (reveal your hand, Blind→Seen), Bet (call the stake — Blind pays the stake, Seen pays double), Raise (increase the stake), or Fold. Teen Patti additionally lets a Seen player request a Side Show — a private hand comparison with the previous Seen player — which the target accepts or declines (the loser folds). When only two players remain you can Show to force a showdown. The last player standing in a deal wins the pot, chip-busted players are eliminated, and the last player with chips wins the match. Hand ranking is Trail (three of a kind) > Pure Sequence (straight flush) > Sequence (straight) > Color (flush) > Pair > High Card.
blurb.terrace: Also called Queen of Italy: the foundations build up in alternating colour, from a rank you pick yourself.
blurb.texasholdembonus: Hold'em decisions, casino tempo. Bonus bets give it a little extra spice.
blurb.thirtyone: Draw, discard, or knock to near 31 in one suit. Lowest loses a life.
blurb.threecard: Three-card high-speed poker. A hand takes seconds; bet variations add depth. A favorite for short-attention nights.
blurb.threecardbrag: A 4-player British vying game and an ancestor of poker, played with a 52-card deck, 3 cards each, plus chips and a pot. Each player is Blind (hasn't looked) or Seen. On your turn: See (reveal your hand, Blind→Seen), Bet (call the stake — Blind pays the stake, Seen pays double), Raise (increase the stake), or Fold. When only two players remain a Seen player can Show to force a showdown. The last player standing in a deal wins the pot, chip-busted players are eliminated, and the last player with chips wins the match. Hand ranking is Prial (three of a kind) > Running Flush > Run > Flush > Pair > High Card, where 3-3-3 is the best Prial and A-2-3 the best Run.
blurb.threecardrummy: A casino game turned upside down: the **lower** your three-card total, the better. Face cards are 10, an ace is 1, and three of a rank or three in suit and sequence count 0 — the best hand there is. The dealer qualifies on 20 or less, so anything under that is worth playing. No hand rankings to memorise; just add up and stay small.
blurb.threethirteen: A two-deck (104-card) Rummy played over 11 rounds. Each round deals one more card (3 up to 13), and a different rank is wild that round. Knock once your whole hand melds; everyone else gets one last turn, then deadwood is tallied. Lowest cumulative score after round 11 wins. For 2 to 4 players.
blurb.tichu: A wildly popular 2-vs-2 partnership game. Daifugo-style combos meet four special cards (Dragon, Phoenix, Dog, Mahjong) and the daring Tichu call.
blurb.tienlen: Vietnam's national card game. Strict suit ranking and bombs that blow away the mighty 2.
blurb.toepen: A Dutch bluffing game on 32 cards, four to a hand, whose ranking is the standard order inverted: the ten is highest and the jack lowest.
blurb.trappola: A 16th-century Venetian/Bohemian four-player partnership trick-taker on a dedicated 36-card pack (A,3,4,5,6,7,J,Q,K), nine cards each with no stock. There is no trump and following suit is mandatory, so the highest card of the led suit always wins. The rank order runs A>K>Q>J>7>6>5>4>3 — the reverse of Tressette, where 3 and 2 are strongest. Combinations held in the dealt hand score automatically.
blurb.trash: Garbage / Trash. Fill ten slots — half solitaire, half social.
blurb.trenteetquarante: A classic Monte-Carlo banking game (Rouge et Noir) with no card decisions. Pick one of four even-money bets — Noir, Rouge, Couleur, or Inverse — and a stake. The dealer deals two rows of cards, Noir (black) then Rouge (red), summing each until it reaches 31 or more; the row with the LOWER total wins. Noir/Rouge bet on which row wins, while Couleur/Inverse bet on whether the color of the first card dealt matches the winning color. A tie at exactly 31 in both rows is a 'Refait' and you lose half your stake. It carries one of the smallest house edges in the casino.
blurb.tressette: One of Italy's big three card games. A no-trump must-follow trick-taker with an unusual 3>2>A ranking and thirds-of-a-point scoring you fight for with your partner.
blurb.trex: A Middle Eastern contract game: each player takes a turn as king, choosing from five contracts until everyone has played all five.
blurb.tripeaks: Three peaks to dismantle. The pick-up rhythm is delicious.
blurb.troggu: Swiss Valais tarot on 78 cards. Each contract changes what winning means, right down to Misere, where you must take nothing.
blurb.truco: A South American / Spanish mind game. Raise the stakes mid-trick and test your opponent's nerve with bluffs.
blurb.tusac: Rummy on a 112-card four-colour deck. No numeric order, so the only combinations are three of one colour, a cross-colour chariot-horse-cannon, and five soldiers.
blurb.tute: A Spanish classic for four in partnerships (2 vs 2). A trump trick-taker on the 40-card deck: hold both K+Q of a suit to declare a 'marriage' for bonus points, or collect four Kings or four Queens to declare 'Tute' for an instant win.
blurb.twentynine: An Indian/Bangladeshi 2-team bidding trick-taker with a hidden trump. Four players (seats 0&2 vs 1&3) get 8 cards each from a 32-card deck (7–A) and play 8 tricks. Bid Pass / 16 / 20 / 24 / 28; the highest bidder's team secretly picks a trump suit that stays hidden until someone can no longer follow. Card points are J=3, 9=2, A=1, 10=1, plus +1 for the last trick — 29 in all; trick rank is J > 9 > A > 10 > K > Q > 8 > 7. Make the bid (capture at least your bid in card points) to score +1 game point, else the other team scores +1. The first team to the target game points (default 6) wins.
blurb.twotenjack: A Japanese Napoleon variant — 2, 10, and J are trump. Distinctive household game.
blurb.tysiac: The classic Polish card game. Three players bid over a 24-card deck for the right to become the Declarer, then exchange through the Talon and try to make the contract. Trump is chosen dynamically by declaring a marriage (King+Queen), which scores 40/60/80/100 by suit. Rank runs A>10>K>Q>J>9, points total 120 per deal, and the first player to reach 1000 wins the match.
blurb.ulti: A 3-player Hungarian contract trick-taker on a 32-card deck (A,10,K,Q,J,9,8,7; trick rank A>10>K>Q>J>9>8>7). You (seat 0) are always the declarer, playing alone against a coalition of two CPU defenders. Ten cards each plus a 2-card talon are dealt; you declare Party (score the most points), Betli (win no trick), or Durchmarsch (win every trick), naming a trump suit for a Party contract. Take the talon, discard two, and play out ten must-follow tricks. Coins are exchanged on the contract's success or failure, and the highest coin balance after the set deals wins the match.
blurb.ultimatetexasholdem: All about when to raise. Hold'em veterans love the timing-of-courage decisions.
blurb.videopoker: Casino-machine solo. Memorize the pay table; the hold/discard decision is the high.
blurb.vint: Russian bridge, played without a dummy -- all four hands stay concealed to the very last trick.
blurb.vira: A 19th-century Swedish auction trick-taker whose pot carries forward — a run of failures makes the next contract worth more.
blurb.war: Just compare top cards. Zero strategy; pure mindless time-passer.
blurb.wasp: A gentler Scorpion: any card can fill an empty column, so it rarely stalls.
blurb.watten: A Bavarian/Austrian 4-player, 2-team trick-taker on a 32-card pack. Five cards are dealt and the dealer declares a Schlag rank plus a critical (trump) suit. The three permanent top trumps are Max (K♥) > Belli (K♦) > Spitz (7♦), then all cards of the Schlag rank, then the critical suit, then plain cards. Teams play five tricks; either team may raise the stake for the other to hold or fold. Win at least three tricks to score the stake — first team to 15 wins.
blurb.whist: Bridge's ancestor — a simple, dignified English trick-taking classic.
blurb.whitehead: An open Klondike variant: every card face-up, but you may only build by the same colour.
blurb.windmill: A two-deck cross: the centre climbs A-K four times over, while the four corners run King down to Ace.
blurb.wizard: Exact-bid trick-taking with a 60-card deck: 4 Wizards (always win) and 4 Jesters (always lose). A modern classic.
blurb.yaniv: Shed cards to drop your hand to 5 or less, then call Yaniv — but beware the Asaf undercut.
blurb.yukon: A Klondike offshoot allowing column-crossing moves. Klondike-vet's next step.
blurb.zheng: Zheng Shangyou (争上游). The traditional Chinese climbing game that fathered Daifugo and Big Two. Four players split a 54-card deck (jokers included) and race to shed their hands, beating the table with singles, pairs, triples, straights, and pair runs — or passing. Strength runs 3<4<…<K<A<2<small joker<big joker, and suits never matter. A four-of-a-kind bomb tops any normal play, and the two-joker bomb beats everything. Finish order sets ranks 1st through 4th.
blurb.zwanzigerrufen: Austrian calling tarock. The declarer calls trump XX and whoever holds it is a secret ally; if everyone passes, taking the most points loses.
blurb.zwicker: A north-German fishing game on 55 cards. Aces and court cards each carry two values and you pick which.
blurb.baccaratbanque: Baccarat Banque is the French form where **one bank plays two tableaux at once**, out of a three-pack shoe. **A loss does not move the bank** - unlike Chemin de Fer, the seat is yours until the shoe runs out or you retire.
