blurb.continentalrummy: Continental Rummy is the rummy where **sets count for nothing**. All fifteen cards must be sequences, and they go down **all at once** - in one of exactly three shapes: 3+3+3+3+3, 4+4+4+3 or 5+4+3+3. **Three fives totals fifteen and is still not a go-out.**

stretch_blurb.accordion: Completion is rare; the journey itself is the joy.
stretch_blurb.acesup: When you want a fast, brainless palate cleanser between heavier games.
stretch_blurb.agnes: Klondike columns, a Canfield base rank, no redeal — tight and tactical.
stretch_blurb.alaska: Keep Yukon's free stack moves, but look for connections running either way.
stretch_blurb.allfours: A pocket-sized trick-taker with a clever beg/stand mind-game and four ways to score.
stretch_blurb.aluette: A 4-player 2v2 trick-taker on a 48-card Spanish pack. No trumps: six named cards outrank everything.
stretch_blurb.americantoad: Empty columns refill from the reserve automatically, and once it is gone only the waste can fill them. One redeal, and that is all.
stretch_blurb.anaconda: Pass three, then two, then one — then roll your best five and bet it out. Wild poker.
stretch_blurb.andarbahar: A pure two-way call. Nothing to decide, so all that is left is the reveal.
stretch_blurb.auldlangsyne: You never choose where a card lands, so luck decides almost everything. Deal again and again.
stretch_blurb.baccarat: Pure gambling. The antidote to decision-fatigue nights.
stretch_blurb.badugi: Short and deep — a lowball-curious onramp.
stretch_blurb.baloot: Two orders and two point tables over the same 32 cards. The strong cards change the moment someone declares.
stretch_blurb.banluck: The bank moves, so everyone takes a turn with the hard job.
stretch_blurb.barbu: A French compendium of 7 mini trick-taking contracts in one game.
stretch_blurb.baseballpoker: The same 3 is a gift in the hole and a bill on the board.
stretch_blurb.basra: An Egyptian/Levantine fishing game on a 52-card deck. Capture table cards by matching rank or summing to your played card; a Jack sweeps the table. Clear the table with a single card for a Basra bonus. Score the 7♦, 10♦, Aces, most cards, and every Basra.
stretch_blurb.bauernschnapsen: An Austrian bidding team game — declare a contract, then follow suit from trick one.
stretch_blurb.beggarmyneighbour: Pure luck. The suspense is in the penalty chain — when will it end?
stretch_blurb.beleagueredcastle: A clean board for computational minds.
stretch_blurb.coinche: Everything turns on whether the number you named is reachable. Double, or redouble.
stretch_blurb.belote: A door into French card culture and its 'bel' announce.
stretch_blurb.bezique: A 2-player melding trick game, the ancestor of Pinochle. Win a trick to declare a meld — marriages, Bezique (♠Q+♦J), or four-of-a-kind — for points, then race to 1000 as the emptied stock flips the game into a strict must-follow endgame.
stretch_blurb.bhabhi: It names a loser, not a winner. Getting out early wins nothing -- only being last loses.
stretch_blurb.bideuchre: A set costs you your BID, not the tricks you took, and the defenders score theirs either way. Naming no trump LOW reverses the ranking so the nine is highest -- a way out with a weak hand.
stretch_blurb.bidwhist: Jokers and a high/low twist drive this American-style partnership battle.
stretch_blurb.bigben: When nothing moves, the stock tops every column back up to three. An emptied column never comes back, so keeping them alive matters.
stretch_blurb.bigo: Five cards, exploding combinations. Nuts-on-nuts Omaha spin-off.
stretch_blurb.bigohilo: Five cards, hi/lo both ways. Peak volatility.
stretch_blurb.bigtwo: Poker-hand climbing from Hong Kong — a fresh angle on shedding games.
stretch_blurb.bisley: Build ascending and descending foundations at once. Everything is visible, and it is still hard.
stretch_blurb.blackhole: Absorb all 52 cards by ±1 rank around a central pile. A fully-visible look-ahead puzzle.
stretch_blurb.blackjack: The 21 instinct may be obvious — but the betting decisions surprise.
stretch_blurb.blackjackswitch: If you can savor the 'wrong-order' regret, this rewards.
stretch_blurb.boston: Piccolissimo asks for EXACTLY one trick -- taking none fails it. On a trick bid you may call a partner and turn it into two against two.
stretch_blurb.botifarra: With so much forced, the moves you do get to choose carry real weight.
stretch_blurb.bouillotte: An 18th-century French salon gamble — call, vie, or fold for the pot with a shared card in play.
stretch_blurb.bourre: Bluff, fold, and grab tricks — but take none after playing and the whole pot is yours to pay.
stretch_blurb.braid: Only the four braid fields consume the braid, and the eight helpers can only be filled from the waste — never emptied back. Both roads run one way.
stretch_blurb.bridge: Worth settling in for — the world's deepest card language.
stretch_blurb.bristol: A tactical fan-and-tableau solitaire for planners.
stretch_blurb.brusquembille: An unusual order — the ten outranks the king.
stretch_blurb.bura: Points never win on their own -- you must claim, and claiming short loses on the spot. There is no obligation to follow suit, so discarding a card you cannot win with is a real move.
stretch_blurb.burraco: Italian Canasta with a hidden 11-card pozzetto twist.
stretch_blurb.calabresella: An Italian Tressette-family trick-taker where one Soloist takes on the other two. Bid chiamo or solo, exchange via the four-card monte, and — with no trump — capture more than half the 33 thirds. Race to 21 in this three-player battle of one vs two.
stretch_blurb.callbreak: South Asia's go-to — a peek at world household games.
stretch_blurb.canasta: Long-form South American Rummy — meld grandeur.
stretch_blurb.caribbeandraw: Caribbean Stud where you can redraw two cards. Draw, or stand pat?
stretch_blurb.caribbeanstud: Chase the jackpot dream against the CPU.
stretch_blurb.carioca: A seven-round South American contract rummy — meet each round's harder sets and runs, shed your hand, and finish with the lowest score.
stretch_blurb.casinoholdem: Hold'em texture for those wary of opponents.
stretch_blurb.catchten: Honor-capture scoring adds a fresh twist to follow-suit trick play.
stretch_blurb.cego: A 4-player Baden trick-taker on the 54-card tarock deck. The declarer chooses Cego (keep one card and swap the rest for the 10-card blind — a gamble) or Handspiel, then plays 1-vs-3. Make the contract by capturing over half the card-points; the highest cumulative score after the set deals wins.
stretch_blurb.chemindefer: Less about the cards you get than the card you choose to take.
stretch_blurb.chinchon: A Spanish Gin Rummy cousin with elimination.
stretch_blurb.chinesepoker: Puzzle lovers will adore splitting 13 cards optimally. Brainy casino.
stretch_blurb.chineseten: Every play also turns a card from the stock, which captures on the same terms. The reds are worth 210 between them, so 105 draws.
stretch_blurb.cinch: A four-player bidding trick-taker on a 52-card deck. Bid 0-14, and the winner names trump and leads. The Left and Right Pedros (the trump 5 and the same-color 5) are worth 5 points each, so 14 points per deal are up for grabs. Miss your bid and you're set back. First to 21 wins this individual-scoring race.
stretch_blurb.cincinnati: Five reveals means five chances to get out cheaply.
stretch_blurb.clocksolitaire: Pure luck — pure deferral of thought.
stretch_blurb.colorado: A solitaire whose only decision is where to dump the waste card, feeding ascending and descending foundations at once.
stretch_blurb.colourwhist: Sometimes the deal simply decides for you.
stretch_blurb.congress: An empty pile can only be filled from the stock or the waste, and there is no redeal — one pass is all you get.
stretch_blurb.conquian: The Mexican grandfather of all Rummy games.
stretch_blurb.contractrummy: Different contracts per round — learn deeper.
stretch_blurb.courchevel: The one Omaha where folding pre-flop has a reason.
stretch_blurb.courtpiece: A South-Asian 2-team trick-taker (Rang) where the caller (Hakim) peeks at 5 cards and names the trump — no bidding. Race to 7 of 13 tricks for a Sar, and sweep the board for a Court bonus in this regal 13-trick duel.
stretch_blurb.crazyeights: Touch the source of UNO — and family warmth.
stretch_blurb.crazyfourpoker: The question is how hard you press when the hand finally comes.
stretch_blurb.crazyquilt: Every card you take opens a neighbour's short side. Finding the order that cascades is the whole puzzle.
stretch_blurb.cribbagesquares: Build eight hands at once without knowing their shared fifth card. Everything rides on how you stack fifteens and pairs.
stretch_blurb.cruel: Random luck test — a light reset.
stretch_blurb.cuarenta: Ecuador's national game for 4 players in 2 teams on a 40-card deck. Match a rank to sweep table cards. Grab the card just laid for a caída (+2), chain three-plus of a rank for a ronda, clear the table for a limpia (+1), and take the majority for +6. First team to 40 wins.
stretch_blurb.cuckoo: A simple 4-player life-survival game. Each holds one card and three lives; on your turn keep or swap with your neighbour. Reveal a King to refuse a swap. The lowest card loses a life, and at zero you're out. Last player standing wins. A.k.a. Chase the Ace.
stretch_blurb.cucumber: Only the final trick scores, so the whole game is about not holding high cards at the end.
stretch_blurb.curdsandwhey: No stock, no foundations — assemble all four suits in place.
stretch_blurb.desmoche: Despite the name, poker rankings play no part. A deal nobody wins leaves the pot standing, so it grows.
stretch_blurb.deuceswild: A gentler entry to Video Poker.
stretch_blurb.deucetoseven: Three draws to chase the lowest hand — deep lowball strategy.
stretch_blurb.diplomat: No same-suit restriction means far more landing spots. When you spend an empty column is the whole game.
stretch_blurb.doppelkopf: Germany's serious partnership trick-taker, played while probing for your hidden allies — with Re/Kontra calls to raise the stakes.
stretch_blurb.doubleattack: The luxury of choosing your stake after the information arrives.
stretch_blurb.doubleklondike: Two-deck Klondike — clear 104 cards to eight foundations. An expanded solitaire needing long look-ahead.
stretch_blurb.doubt: Remember the joy of catching a bluff.
stretch_blurb.doudizhu: One Landlord vs two Peasants — bombs, rockets, and strategic cooperation make every hand explosive.
stretch_blurb.dragontiger: Asian casino air in three minutes.
stretch_blurb.dramaha: Two hands from one holding — every discard cuts both ways.
stretch_blurb.duchess: While any reserve remains, an empty column can only be filled from it — a hole is the reserve's exit, not a digging tool.
stretch_blurb.durak: Russian originality — once you've got the rules, you can't stop.
stretch_blurb.easthaven: More strategic than Klondike, quicker than Spider — a connoisseur's solitaire.
stretch_blurb.ecarte: A 2-player French 32-card trick game built around an Exchange phase of propose, accept-or-refuse, and discard-and-draw bluffing before 5 strict must-follow tricks. Take 3 for a point, sweep all 5 (Vole) for two, and race to a target of 5.
stretch_blurb.egyptianratscrew: Slap Jack evolved — reflexes one notch up.
stretch_blurb.eightoff: Once FreeCell is familiar, step here.
stretch_blurb.escoba: A Spanish fishing game where you capture to a sum of 15; the solo play feels fresh.
stretch_blurb.estimation: Too many hurts as much as too few. Throwing away a winner to avoid one extra trick is the whole feel of it.
stretch_blurb.euchre: The Midwest's tight, smart trick-taking primer.
stretch_blurb.faro: A 19th-century American saloon banking game, player vs bank. Place chips on an A–K layout (copper = bet to lose) and the bank turns two cards at a time. The first (losing) card is collected, the second (winning) card pays 1:1, and a same-rank split lets the bank take half. Call the order of the last three cards for a 4:1 payout.
stretch_blurb.fiftyone: Cap-management is a rare mechanic worth a try.
stretch_blurb.fivecardstud: Poker's oldest stud form — a simple yet deep classic.
stretch_blurb.fivehundred: Euchre's bowers crossed with Bridge-style bidding — a deep, rewarding classic.
stretch_blurb.flowergarden: Six open flower beds, a one-way bouquet, suit-ignored packing.
stretch_blurb.followthequeen: The best hand at the table can change the instant the wild rank moves. One card rewrites every read.
stretch_blurb.fortress: Foundations start empty — scan all ten columns for a same-suit link.
stretch_blurb.fortyandeight: Forty Thieves with one redeal — austere, but a little kinder.
stretch_blurb.fortyfives: An Irish/Canadian 2-team bidding trick-taker where the 5, J, and ♥A reign as top trumps you can even hold back (Reneging). Bid 15, 20, or 25 (Jink) and partner up for the tricks.
stretch_blurb.fortythieves: Sometimes you can't win — the austere classic.
stretch_blurb.fourcardpoker: Flip between player/dealer betting — fresh perspective.
stretch_blurb.fourseasons: Foundations that do not start at Ace, and ranks that wrap. One changed assumption, a different game.
stretch_blurb.fourteenout: No redeal, so when a pair can be made two ways, choosing the wrong one is how you lose.
stretch_blurb.freebet: A single round teaches you what free really costs.
stretch_blurb.frenchtarot: A 4-player trick-taker on the 78-card tarot deck. Win the auction (Petite / Garde / Garde Sans / Garde Contre), exchange the 6-card chien, and capture a bouts-based point target across the tricks. Contract multipliers scale the deal score; the highest cumulative score wins.
stretch_blurb.gaigel: A Swabian team marriage game — declare King+Queen and race to 101.
stretch_blurb.ganjifa: A Mughal-era Indian 3-player trick-taker on a circular 96-card, 8-suit deck. Its signature is that rank strength inverts between suit groups.
stretch_blurb.germanwhist: A two-player game of repeatedly declining to win. The hand you hold entering the second half decides everything.
stretch_blurb.golf: If TriPeaks works, this completes the set.
stretch_blurb.gongzhu: Chinese Hearts where positive and negative points collide — the doubler and exposure send scores swinging wildly.
stretch_blurb.goofspiel: A game-theory staple with no turn order -- it is all in how you spend thirteen cards.
stretch_blurb.gostop: The Korean version of Koi-Koi. Capture same-month field cards on the 48-card hanafuda deck and score in five categories — Gwang, Godori, Tti, Yeol, and Pi. Reach the target score, then choose go (continue) or stop (bank), where go raises the stakes but risks the gwang-bak, pi-bak, and go-bak penalties.
stretch_blurb.grandfathersclock: One o'clock ends on an Ace, twelve on a Queen. The layout is the goal.
stretch_blurb.guandan: **The level cards beat aces**, and the two hearts among them are wild. The finishing order sets both the next hand's tribute and the climb: first and second is worth four levels, and no result is ever worth three.
stretch_blurb.guts: A nerve-fueled In/Out showdown for the pot — over in seconds, tense every time.
stretch_blurb.hachihachi: The classic three-player Japanese hanafuda game on a 48-card flower deck. Capture field cards of the same month, then score captured piles by card points (Bright 20 / Animal 10 / Ribbon 5 / Chaff 1) plus yaku such as the Brights and Boar-Deer-Butterfly. No koi-koi/stop decision — each player settles vs the 88 baseline and the highest cumulative score wins.
stretch_blurb.handandfoot: Two-stage Canasta: play your hand, then your foot.
stretch_blurb.hasenpfeffer: Bidding is compulsory -- once three pass the dealer cannot, so no hand is thrown in.
stretch_blurb.hokm: The hakem picks trump from five cards and keeps the role while winning. A shut-out (Kot) counts double.
stretch_blurb.honeymoonbridge: Thirteen tricks that score nothing rebuild your hand -- then the real game starts.
stretch_blurb.horse: Being good at one game is not enough — you have to play all five.
stretch_blurb.indianpoker: Online loses some of the magic, but the mechanic is still fun.
stretch_blurb.indianrummy: India's 13-card Rummy; pure sequences are key.
stretch_blurb.irishpoker: Bridges Omaha's four-card power with Hold'em's two-card showdown.
stretch_blurb.ironcross: One irreversible choice per hand, and the centre card lands last.
stretch_blurb.israeliwhist: What you win at auction is the right to choose trump, not the contract. An exact call rises with its square.
stretch_blurb.jass: A taste of Swiss card culture and the clever 'Schieben' pass.
stretch_blurb.jokerpoker: A lab for learning wild-card timing.
stretch_blurb.schafkopf: Choosing the contract is choosing what counts as trump. Call a partner, or go it alone.
stretch_blurb.julepe: A Spanish betting hand that turns on one question: enter or drop. Fall short and your next stake doubles.
stretch_blurb.kaiser: Only the winning bidder sees the two-card kitty -- but neither scoring card may be discarded, so a three of spades has to be forced onto somebody.
stretch_blurb.karnoffel: The highest card is the JACK (the Karnöffel), not the six. The seven (the devil) beats everything but the Karnöffel ONLY WHEN LED, and loses to every card otherwise. The 3, 4 and 5 are trumps that still lose to face cards.
stretch_blurb.unsunkaruta: A suit where the one is the strongest, and a rule you have to ask for.
stretch_blurb.quodlibet: Twelve contracts where winning tricks is sometimes right and sometimes ruinous — and one where your own hand is hidden from you alone.
stretch_blurb.dehlapakad: Winning a trick gives you nothing. Win two in a row and the whole centre pile — tens and all — is yours.
stretch_blurb.sutda: Two cards, one bet. Only months 1, 3 and 8 carry a bright, so the top hand has exactly three forms.
stretch_blurb.cirulla: Three ways to capture at once, and one ace can take the whole table if no ace is lying on it.
stretch_blurb.diloti: Greek fishing where declarations build piles and a one-card sweep, the xeri, is worth ten.
stretch_blurb.comet: The ancestor of the stops family: sequences climb by rank ignoring suit, with a wild 9♦.
stretch_blurb.costlycolours: The ancestor of Cribbage: the count pays at 15, 25 and 31, and colours top the show.
stretch_blurb.kemps: A 4-player team game of secret signals. Swap cards through a shared field to collect four of a kind, then shout "Kemps!" when your partner flashes the signal — or call "Counter-Kemps!" if you read the opponents. First team to 5 wins.
stretch_blurb.kille: Challenge the Cuckoo and the round ends on the spot; challenge the Hussar and you are the one who goes out. A Harlequin handed to you in an exchange is the lowest card, not the highest.
stretch_blurb.king: A four-player trick-avoidance compendium: seven deals, seven contracts, and a simple goal — don't take the cards that hurt. Score the fewest penalties across the match to win.
stretch_blurb.kingalbert: Open columns, a one-way reserve, alternate-color packing.
stretch_blurb.kingo: Three alike shows up 0.4% of the time. You do not aim for it.
stretch_blurb.klaberjass: Only the better sequence scores -- but it scores every run its holder has. Fail to beat your opponent as maker and the whole hand goes to them.
stretch_blurb.klaverjas: A serious Dutch trump trick-taker with forced overtrumping and Roem bonuses. Partner up and fight over card points in a step-up of strategic depth.
stretch_blurb.klondike: The reigning solitaire — comforting and reliable.
stretch_blurb.knockoutwhist: A British survival trick-taker with a hand that shrinks every round — win zero tricks and you're knocked out. One Dogbone buys a single second chance as you race to be the last one standing.
stretch_blurb.koenigrufen: An Austrian 4-player trick-taker on the 54-card tarock deck. The declarer who wins the Rufer auction calls a King, making its holder a secret partner. Exchange the 6-card talon and capture card-points to make the contract. Highest cumulative score after the set deals wins.
stretch_blurb.koikoi: A two-player Japanese hanafuda matching game on a 48-card flower deck. Capture field cards of the same month with your hand and stock draws to form 'yaku' such as the Brights, Boar-Deer-Butterfly, Ribbons, Animals, and Chaff. Each completed yaku lets you call koi-koi (continue) or shobu (stop and score).
stretch_blurb.labellelucie: A classic fan solitaire with just three gather-and-reshuffle redeals to escape a dead end.
stretch_blurb.laughandliedown: A hand laid down becomes everyone else prey. You settle on captured cards against eight, so one more card is worth chasing.
stretch_blurb.lingerlonger: You are dealt only as many cards as there are players -- keep winning and your hand never shrinks.
stretch_blurb.literature: Winning takes FIVE of eight — a majority. Four decides nothing, since the other side can reach four too. A claim has three outcomes: misnaming which teammate holds a card CANCELS the half-suit rather than handing it over.
stretch_blurb.loba: A knockout: reach 101 penalty points and you are out. Going out in one go without melding first takes ten off.
stretch_blurb.loo: An English pot-based gambling trick-taker. Five cards each, the turn-up sets trump, and you choose to play or pass. Participants fight five must-follow / must-head tricks, each worth one-fifth of the pot. Take no trick and you're 'looed', paying a penalty into the next deal. No target score — just build up chips.
stretch_blurb.macau: Crazy Eights with bite — penalty stacks make it a party.
stretch_blurb.machiavelli: Italy's Rummy; rearrange the shared table.
stretch_blurb.madrasso: A Veneto four-hander where the deal itself fixes the trump, and the richest card is the strongest.
stretch_blurb.manille: A French/Belgian trump trick-taker with a twist: the 10 is the strongest card. Partner up and fight over card points in this clean, declaration-free classic.
stretch_blurb.mao: Crazy Eights with a twist — deduce the secret rule.
stretch_blurb.marias: A Czech/Slovak three-player trick-taker where a rotating Soloist takes on the other two. Marriages and a final-trick bonus drive this tense one-vs-all classic.
stretch_blurb.memory: Memory drill — generations get along here.
stretch_blurb.mendikot: Nobody chooses trump. The first card that cannot follow suit sets it.
stretch_blurb.michigan: Stake chips on four boodle cards, then race to play ascending suit runs and empty your hand for the pot.
stretch_blurb.mighty: The game to play with your Korean friends.
stretch_blurb.minchiate: A 4-player 2v2 trick-taker on Florence's 97-card tarot deck. Its signature is the 40-trump ladder, the longest here.
stretch_blurb.minibridge: Everyone shows how strong their hand is before a card is played -- the gentlest way into bridge.
stretch_blurb.mississippistud: The middle ground between tempo and depth.
stretch_blurb.missmilligan: Empty columns take only Kings, and once the stock is gone your only escape is holding a run aside.
stretch_blurb.montebank: One number decides every choice — nothing else to hide behind.
stretch_blurb.mrsmop: No luck at all — whether it can be won is settled at the deal; the rest is reading.
stretch_blurb.mus: A bluffing duel where hands stay hidden. Team up and gamble big with Órdago — a Basque classic for lovers of mind games.
stretch_blurb.mushi: Unlike koi-koi there is no stop decision: you play the hand out. The score is your margin over an even split of the pack's 230 points.
stretch_blurb.nainjaune: The yellow dwarf in the centre takes five chips a deal. You settle in points rather than cards, so every court card left is a ten-point debt.
stretch_blurb.nap: A British classic gambling trick-taker: declare 2–5 of your 5 tricks and go it alone to make the contract. Chase the one-shot high payout of a Nap.
stretch_blurb.napoleonssquare: Eight foundations to grow at once. How you bundle the runs decides the endgame.
stretch_blurb.narcotic: The redeal never shuffles — when a board comes back around with no move, that is the end.
stretch_blurb.nertz: Simultaneous solitaire combat. Hands and head both busy.
stretch_blurb.ninetynine: Your bid is hidden in the cards you bury — pure strategy.
stretch_blurb.niuniu: A last digit of zero is Niu Niu and pays triple; no valid triple at all is a no-bull, the weakest. There is nothing to decide — the bet settles the round.
stretch_blurb.oasispoker: Once Caribbean Stud feels too tame, slide here.
stretch_blurb.ohhell: The 'exact bid' tension is a luck-skill tightrope.
stretch_blurb.oichokabu: One small draw-or-stand call, then pure kabufuda tension.
stretch_blurb.oldmaid: Five minutes of childhood — for one more laugh.
stretch_blurb.omaha: Hold'em players' next horizon. Different mental work.
stretch_blurb.ombre: The classic Spanish trick-taker of Baroque Europe. Three players, one Ombre against a coalition of two. Bid entrar or solo, name trump, and win the most of nine tricks. Beware Codille — when an opponent beats you, the penalty doubles.
stretch_blurb.openfacechinese: Open Face Chinese Poker for 2 to 4 players vs the CPU. Cards are dealt one at a time and placed irrevocably into a Top (3), Middle (5) or Bottom (5) row. Keep the rows in non-decreasing strength or foul. Win rows against opponents, earn royalty bonuses, and chase Fantasyland with a strong Top row. Highest total after the target rounds wins.
stretch_blurb.osmosis: A fresh seep-rule puzzle for lateral thinkers.
stretch_blurb.paigow: For when you want time at the table to think.
stretch_blurb.pan: A large 8-deck (320-card) Mexican rummy — lay down sets and ropes, earn chips, and race to meld eleven cards first.
stretch_blurb.pasur: Face cards never join the sum -- the ones left on the table quietly reshape the endgame.
stretch_blurb.penguin: FreeCell family, base rank changes each deal.
stretch_blurb.perseverance: The redeal never shuffles — the order you leave behind is the board you get back.
stretch_blurb.pig: Nothing to grab and nothing to score -- being slow to notice is the only way to lose.
stretch_blurb.pineapple: Where Hold'em vets play with discard decisions.
stretch_blurb.pinochle: An American mid-tier classic to peek at.
stretch_blurb.pishti: A Turkish 2–4 player fishing game. Match the pile's top rank — or play a wild Jack — to sweep the whole pile. Capturing a lone card scores a Pişti (+10, or +20 for Jack on Jack). Re-deal until the stock is gone, then total most cards, Aces, 2♣, 10♦, Jacks and Pişti bonuses for the highest score.
stretch_blurb.pitch: A taste of regional American card culture.
stretch_blurb.poch: Pools nobody claims carry over and swell. The last stage runs each suit upwards, and going out collects from every hand still holding cards.
stretch_blurb.poker: Classic five-card draw — the psyche template.
stretch_blurb.polignac: Just four dangerous cards. Everything rides on working out who is holding which jack.
stretch_blurb.pontoon: You cannot stick below 15, and buying is dead once you twist. Make a pontoon and you take the bank.
stretch_blurb.popejoan: The dealer dresses eight compartments with fifteen chips and a turn-up sets trumps. Holding the Pope excuses you from paying when someone goes out.
stretch_blurb.preference: A Russian/Austrian classic 3-player trick-taker where a bid crowns one declarer to take on the other two alone. Read the table across the Six, Misère, Seven, and Eight contracts.
stretch_blurb.primero: A Renaissance ancestor of poker — call, vie, or fold for the pot with four cards and pure nerve.
stretch_blurb.prsi: A Czech pub classic — leaner Crazy Eights with stacking 7s.
stretch_blurb.put: Fold or see it — there is no re-raise.
stretch_blurb.quadrille: Ombre for four. The winning bidder calls a king for a partner — but nobody knows who it is until that king is played.
stretch_blurb.germansolo: Until the called ace hits the table, nobody knows whose side they are on.
stretch_blurb.gleek: Auction, ruff, melds, tricks. One deal, four separate contests.
stretch_blurb.rams: Every round asks one question: is this hand worth entering? Knowing when to fold is the whole skill.
stretch_blurb.ramsch: Sweep all ten tricks for a Durchmarsch and the table pays you instead. The only way to attack in a game about refusing.
stretch_blurb.rankandfile: No redeal — every card you turn from the stock has to be spent or lost.
stretch_blurb.razz: Winning with weak hands — a useful mental flip.
stretch_blurb.reddog: Under five minutes per round. A pure micro-snack.
stretch_blurb.reversis: You are not aiming for zero — only for fewer than the other three. Somebody always carries those 40 points.
stretch_blurb.rikken: Choosing your contract is the whole game; passing is a skill too.
stretch_blurb.ristikontra: You and your partner win on your combined card count.
stretch_blurb.rollingstone: High cards are a liability here -- the punishment is being given cards, not taking them.
stretch_blurb.rook: A 4-player, 2-team point-trick game on a special 57-card deck (four colors ×1–14 plus the Rook bird). Win the auction, declare a trump color in the nest exchange, and capture point cards in tricks. The first team to 500 wins.
stretch_blurb.royalcotillion: Digging the reserve buys you options, but emptying one costs a slot forever. That single trade is the game.
stretch_blurb.rummy500: American household Rummy in mid-length form.
stretch_blurb.russianbank: A two-deck head-to-head competitive solitaire vs the CPU; first to empty their reserve wins.
stretch_blurb.russianpoker: For the day you want maximum decisions per hand.
stretch_blurb.sakura: Hanafuda without memorising a single yaku. Just count.
stretch_blurb.saliclaw: Columns never build on each other. The only escape is a column holding just its king, so the order you spend those decides the game.
stretch_blurb.samba: Three-deck Canasta — thrilling seven-card same-suit sambas.
stretch_blurb.scarto: A 3-player Italian tarocchi on the 78-card tarot deck. No bidding or partnership — the dealer buries three low cards, then the three play out the tricks. Each deal is a zero-sum settlement against the average of captured card-points; the highest cumulative score wins.
stretch_blurb.piedmontesetarot: Same 78 cards, a different count: 78 points taken three at a time.
stretch_blurb.schnapsen: A two-player duel for the patient strategist.
stretch_blurb.scopa: An Italian fishing game; one card captures the table.
stretch_blurb.scopone: Scopa for two teams; capturing in sync with your partner adds depth.
stretch_blurb.sedma: A Czech/Slovak no-trump capture trick-taker. Play any card, capture with a rank match or a 7, and time your wild 7s to steal the point-rich tricks in this 4-player, 2-team classic.
stretch_blurb.sergeantmajor: Overshoot and you score; fall short and your best cards leave next round.
stretch_blurb.setteemezzo: The king of coins is wild for 0.5 to 7, and you can keep changing it until you stand. Land exactly on 7.5 and you take the bank.
stretch_blurb.sevencardstud: Touch poker's roots — the classic seven-card form.
stretch_blurb.sevencardstudhilo: High and low come from the same seven cards, so chasing both — the scoop — is the greedy line worth learning.
stretch_blurb.chicago: Chase the hand, or sit on the ace of spades and wait for your half.
stretch_blurb.eightgame: Eight rule sets, one stack. Survive the ones you are bad at.
stretch_blurb.sevens: Read the table flow — deeper than it looks.
stretch_blurb.seventwentyseven: A-A-5 makes both 7 and 27. Scooping the whole pot with one hand is the shot you play for.
stretch_blurb.shamrocks: One deal, no redeals — the three-card cap is what runs you out of room.
stretch_blurb.sheepshead: A hidden-partner battle where you may not know who's on your side. For strategists who love deep reads.
stretch_blurb.shelem: Only the A, 10 and 5 score, for exactly 100 a round — and the bidding starts at 100 for that same hundred.
stretch_blurb.shengji: **Trumps are not just the trump suit** -- every card of the level rank, in all four suits, plus all four jokers. The **defenders** collect the points; the declarers win by holding them under 80. And the eight-card kitty reaches the defenders **multiplied** if they take the last trick.
stretch_blurb.shortdeck: Bored of Hold'em? Try inverted hand strengths.
stretch_blurb.simplesimon: An easier, fully-open Spider-family solitaire with no stock — a visible puzzle to solve.
stretch_blurb.sirtommy: Once a card is placed it cannot be moved. Every decision is where to discard it - nothing else.
stretch_blurb.sixbidsolo: A misere asks for zero card POINTS, not zero tricks -- a trick of nines and lower is harmless. A plain bid must exceed 60, so 61, and the payment is the difference from 60 rather than a flat win.
stretch_blurb.sixcardgolf: Match ranks in a column for 0 points! Compete over 9 rounds
stretch_blurb.sjavs: You bid the LENGTH of your trump suit, not a target score. A rubber counts down from 24 and the first side to reach zero takes it.
stretch_blurb.skitgubbe: What you collect becomes your next hand, so winning too much hurts. Equal ranks leave the cards on the table until someone settles it.
stretch_blurb.slobberhannes: Eight tricks of declining to win, for four players. It comes down to whether you kept a low card for the end.
stretch_blurb.slyfox: You commit twenty placements before you may harvest any of them, and burying is one-way — reading which slot you can afford to spend is the game.
stretch_blurb.snap: One card showing is never a snap -- the game only starts when there is something to match.
stretch_blurb.soko: One extra rung in the rankings changes every fold decision. A twist for stud regulars.
stretch_blurb.solowhist: A British classic where a bid crowns one declarer to take on the other three alone. Read the table across Solo, Misère, and Abundance contracts.
stretch_blurb.somerset: No free cells, no stock — hunt alternating-colour runs across all ten columns.
stretch_blurb.spades: Team trick-taking, with no real-life partner required.
stretch_blurb.spanish21: Want one more flavor on top of BlackJack? Here you go.
stretch_blurb.speculation: Sell now or hold on — decided by how many cards are still face down.
stretch_blurb.spiderette: Compact Spider — the right size for a break.
stretch_blurb.spiteandmalice: Two-player race — solitaire fans' onramp to multiplayer.
stretch_blurb.spoilfive: An Irish 5-player trick-taker where the trump 5, J, and ♥A reign supreme and can be held back (Reneging). Win 3 tricks to grab the pot, or it spoils and carries over — pure pot-race tension.
stretch_blurb.spoons: A frantic 4-player party speed game. Pass cards round and round, then lunge for a spoon the instant you hit four of a kind. Miss out and you collect a letter — S, P, O, O, N, S — and six letters knocks you out. Pure reflexes and nerve.
stretch_blurb.stalactites: All four cells start occupied — build suit-agnostic wrapping runs to escape.
stretch_blurb.stealingbundles: An unusual design where already-scored cards can still be attacked -- nothing is ever safe.
stretch_blurb.sthelena: On the first deal a column only reaches the foundation row beside it. The first redeal lifts that, so when you spend it matters.
stretch_blurb.sueca: A clean, declaration-free trump trick-taker. Partner up and fight over card points with must-follow play — the national game of Portugal and Brazil.
stretch_blurb.sultan: Build eight Kings up to their Queens — an ornate two-deck patience.
stretch_blurb.tablanet: A Balkan fishing game on a 52-card deck. Capture table cards by matching rank or summing to your played card; a Jack sweeps the table. Clear the table with a single card for a Tabla bonus. Score the 10♦, 2♣, Aces, Jacks, most cards, and every Tabla.
stretch_blurb.tarabish: In trump, strength and point value stop agreeing. Counting the 20-point jack and 14-point nine is the whole game.
stretch_blurb.tarocchini: A 4-player 2v2 trick-taker on Bologna's 62-card tarot deck. Its signature: four equal-ranking papi where the later-played one wins.
stretch_blurb.teendopaanch: Overshooting scores nothing -- it buys an opponent's best cards next round instead.
stretch_blurb.teenpatti: The Indian variant of Three Card Brag. With just 3 cards each, the real game is whether you dare bet Blind without looking. See, Bet, Raise, Fold — or call a private Side Show against the previous Seen player — then take the pot and bust your rivals out.
stretch_blurb.terrace: The eleven-card terrace feeds the foundations and nothing else, and never refills. Stall it and the game is over.
stretch_blurb.thirtyone: Pub survival game — race to 31, don't be lowest.
stretch_blurb.threecard: An onramp for the poker-shy. Thirty seconds per hand.
stretch_blurb.threecardbrag: A 4-player British vying game and ancestor of poker. With just 3 cards each, the real game is whether you dare bet Blind without looking. See, Bet, Raise, Fold, or Show — then take the pot and bust your rivals out.
stretch_blurb.threecardrummy: You win by not making points. Thirty seconds that invert every poker instinct.
stretch_blurb.threethirteen: An 11-round Rummy where the deal and the wild rank both grow.
stretch_blurb.tichu: Read your partner without a word. Special cards and the Tichu call set up huge swings — race to 1000.
stretch_blurb.tienlen: Vietnamese Big Two — suit order matters and chops topple the 2.
stretch_blurb.toepen: Everyone who misses the final trick pays. A toep raises the stake at any moment, and folding costs the stake before the raise. Ten lives lost and you are out.
stretch_blurb.trappola: A trumpless 16th-century four-hander. The combinations you are dealt score on their own.
stretch_blurb.trenteetquarante: A Monte-Carlo banking game (Rouge et Noir). Pick an even-money bet — Noir, Rouge, Couleur, or Inverse — then the dealer deals two rows to 31+ and the lower row wins. A tie at 31 is a 'Refait' that costs half your stake. One of the smallest house edges around.
stretch_blurb.tressette: Pure no-trump must-follow play with a flipped 3>2>A ranking and partner signalling — an Italian classic.
stretch_blurb.trex: Four contracts punish and the dominoes pay. The 500 in penalties and the 500 paid out cancel, so every game sums to zero.
stretch_blurb.tripeaks: The rhythm-strip joy of pickup solitaires.
stretch_blurb.troggu: Contracts that play to win, and contracts that play to lose.
stretch_blurb.truco: Strong hand or weak, one call sends the points soaring. Read and bluff your way to 15.
stretch_blurb.tusac: Laying a combination is final — what you hold back is the game.
stretch_blurb.tute: A partnership trump trick-taker where marriages and a 'Tute' call can swing the score fast — a Spanish classic for two-team play.
stretch_blurb.twentynine: An Indian/Bangladeshi 2-team trick-taker where the bid-winning team picks a hidden trump nobody sees until you can't follow suit. Chase the 28 card points (the J=3 is king) and read the concealed trump in this tense 8-trick duel.
stretch_blurb.twotenjack: Japanese household nostalgia with quirky trumps.
stretch_blurb.tysiac: The classic Polish trick-taker. Bid for the contract, exchange via the Talon, and set trump with marriages worth 40/60/80/100. Race to 1000 in this three-player battle of nerve.
stretch_blurb.ulti: A 3-player Hungarian contract trick-taker on a 32-card deck. You are always the declarer against a coalition of two CPU players. Declare Party, Betli, or Durchmarsch, exchange two talon cards, and fight ten tricks — coins change hands on whether your contract is made.
stretch_blurb.ultimatetexasholdem: Hold'em veterans wince and grin at the raise-timing.
stretch_blurb.videopoker: The platonic ideal of solo casino.
stretch_blurb.vint: Defenders score for every trick they take, so points accrue even when you cannot beat the contract. Spades are the LOWEST denomination, the reverse of bridge.
stretch_blurb.vira: Three players, thirteen tricks. Each bids once from Gask, Solo, Misère or Vira; the highest bidder plays alone against the other two. Everyone antes into the pot each round: make the contract and you take the whole pot, fail and you add to it for whoever bids next.
stretch_blurb.watten: An Alpine 4-player, 2-team trick-taker built on the Max/Belli/Spitz top trumps and a tense raise / hold / fold stake duel.
stretch_blurb.whist: A clean warm-up before learning Bridge.
stretch_blurb.whitehead: Nothing is hidden — the constraint is that only same-colour runs connect.
stretch_blurb.windmill: There is one rescue — pull a corner card back to the centre — and after using it you must play a sail or waste card before you can use it again.
stretch_blurb.wizard: Always-win Wizards and always-lose Jesters put your reading skills to the test.
stretch_blurb.yaniv: Addictive Israeli hand-reduction game — call Yaniv, dodge the Asaf penalty.
stretch_blurb.yukon: Klondike vets — your next step up.
stretch_blurb.zheng: The Chinese ancestor of Daifugo — suits never matter, and bombs or the joker bomb can flip the table.
stretch_blurb.zwanzigerrufen: Twelve tricks without knowing who is on your side.
stretch_blurb.zwicker: Clearing the table is a "Zwick", worth 1. A deal pays exactly 30, and level card counts leave the majority three unawarded.
stretch_blurb.baccaratbanque: One bank against a right and a left tableau; a loss never costs you the seat.
stretch_blurb.continentalrummy: No sets at all - fifteen cards of pure sequences, laid down in one move.
